CA-AB1170.summary: AB 1170 is California's annual code maintenance bill. It makes nonsubstantive technical changes across various code provisions to carry out the Legislative Counsel's recommendations for maintaining the codes. It was signed and chaptered as Chapter 67, Statutes of 2025, on July 28, 2025.
mechanics: Implements the existing statutory duty of the Legislative Counsel to advise the Legislature on legislation needed to maintain the codes.
Makes only nonsubstantive changes, such as corrections, conforming edits and cleanup, according to the official abstract.
Affects unspecified 'various provisions of the law'. The full text was not available, so the specific code sections amended cannot be confirmed here.
Enacted as Chapter 67, Statutes of 2025, chaptered 2025-07-28.
CA-AB1170.comparison: No comparable bills from other states were listed. This is a routine housekeeping vehicle rather than a gaming policy bill, and it is unusual only in that it may touch many code sections at once without changing their legal effect.
CA-AB1170.watch: Check the chaptered text to see whether any technical edits land in Penal Code gambling provisions, the Gambling Control Act (Bus. & Prof. Code §19800 et seq.) or horse-racing wagering statutes, so that compliance citations and internal references stay accurate.

CA-AB831.summary: AB 831 (Chapter 623, Statutes of 2025) makes it a misdemeanor to operate, conduct, or offer an online sweepstakes game in California. It also makes it a crime for payment processors, financial institutions, geolocation providers, gaming content suppliers, platform providers, and media affiliates to knowingly and willfully support or promote one. It also expands California's existing unfair-practices rules for contests and sweepstakes so they expressly reach internet websites and online apps, and it redefines simulated gambling to include examples such as lottery games, bingo, and sports wagering.
mechanics: Unfair-practice expansion: the existing ban on electronic simulated-gambling methods tied to sweepstakes prizes now expressly covers 'any method, including an internet website or an online application.' The term 'gambling-themed games' is deleted, and 'gambling' is redefined to include examples such as lottery games, bingo, sports wagering, or any game that mimics or simulates similar gambling.

Payment-system trigger: it is an unfair practice to offer such games using a payment system that lets a person play a simulated gambling program for direct or indirect consideration, with eligibility for a prize, cash or cash equivalents, or a chance to win them. This applies in a business establishment, on the internet, or via an online app. Games that do not award cash prizes or cash equivalents are expressly not made unlawful.
New crime: it is unlawful for any person or entity to operate, conduct, or offer an online sweepstakes game (as defined in the bill) in California.

Secondary liability: any entity, financial institution, payment processor, geolocation provider, gaming content supplier, platform provider, or media affiliate that knowingly and willfully supports, directly or indirectly, the operation, conduct, or promotion of an online sweepstakes game in the state is also liable.
Penalties: misdemeanor punishable by a fine of $1,000 to $25,000, up to one year in county jail, or both. The bill creates a state-mandated local program with no reimbursement required.

Carve-outs: lawful games and methods of gambling enterprises licensed under the Gambling Control Act, and California State Lottery operations, are exempt. So are limited, occasional promotional sweepstakes by for-profit businesses that are incidental to substantial bona fide sales of consumer products or services and are not a vehicle for ongoing gambling.
CA-AB831.comparison: The closest analogue on the list is AR HB 1861, which makes operating an illegal online casino or sports betting a felony within a broader interactive gaming framework. AB 831 is narrower in target (online sweepstakes games) and lighter in penalty (misdemeanor), but it reaches further down the supply chain by naming payment processors, geolocation vendors, content suppliers, platforms, and media affiliates. Unlike GA HB 686, HI HB 2570, and HI HB 1308, which would legalize and tax sports wagering, AB 831 authorizes nothing; it is purely prohibitive. KY HB 904, by contrast, regulates rather than bans an adjacent contest product (fantasy contests).
CA-AB831.watch: Watch the 'knowingly and willfully' secondary-liability clause and the express inclusion of sports wagering in the simulated-gambling definition, because vendors, payment partners, and media affiliates that also serve sweepstakes-model or prize-based sports products face misdemeanor exposure in California, where sports betting remains unlicensed and the exemption covers only Gambling Control Act licensees and the State Lottery.

IA-SSB1240.summary: SSB 1240 (renumbered SF 660) appropriates a total of $22 million from Iowa's sports wagering receipts fund (Code section 8.57I) for FY 2025-2026: $14 million to the Department of Education for an education support personnel pay supplement distributed to school districts by enrollment, and $8 million to the Department of Public Safety for the public safety equipment fund. It does not change sports wagering tax rates, licensing, or operator obligations.
mechanics: Sec. 1: $14,000,000 from the sports wagering receipts fund to the Department of Education for FY 2025-2026 to supplement compensation of education support personnel, defined as regular and part-time non-salaried school district employees.

Each district's share equals $14,000,000 multiplied by its FY 2024-25 budget enrollment divided by the statewide total budget enrollment. Districts must report support-personnel data to the department on or before July 1, 2025 to qualify.
The funds are treated as miscellaneous income under section 257.2, are excluded from district cost computations under chapter 257, and are paid on the foundation aid schedule under section 257.16.
Sec. 2: $8,000,000 from the same fund to the Department of Public Safety for deposit in the public safety equipment fund (section 80.48).
Sec. 3: the education appropriation takes effect upon enactment. The public safety appropriation follows the normal effective date.
Per the explanation, the fund is fed by the internet fantasy sports contest tax (Code 99E.6) and the sports wagering net receipts tax (Code 99F.11(5)).
IA-SSB1240.comparison: No comparable bills from other states are listed. The bill is a routine appropriation of existing sports wagering and fantasy sports tax revenue. It is notable mainly because it earmarks wagering receipts for non-gaming purposes (school support staff pay and police equipment) rather than for problem-gambling or regulatory programs, and it leaves the underlying tax structure untouched.
IA-SSB1240.watch: Operators face no direct new obligations here, but growing legislative reliance on sports wagering receipts for recurring education and public safety spending could build pressure to raise the 99F.11 net receipts tax rate in future sessions.

GA-HB686.summary: HB 686 (House Higher Education Committee substitute, LC 56 0648S) would legalize online-only sports betting in Georgia, with the Georgia Lottery Corporation acting as both regulator and "master sports betting licensee." It caps the market at 16 Type 1 licenses, most tied to Georgia pro teams and sports venues, and imposes a 27.5% privilege tax on adjusted gross income, with proceeds going to a dedicated trust fund for the constitutionally specified purposes. The bill has a contingent effective date tied to Georgia constitutional provisions, and it died after being reported favorably by substitute on 2026-03-06.
mechanics: Market structure (50-27-133): no more than 16 Type 1 licenses. Five are reserved for qualifying Georgia pro teams (baseball, football, men's and women's basketball, soccer). One each goes to a 30-year PGA-tour tournament body, a 30-year invitational golf facility, a NASCAR track owner, and the Lottery Corporation. The remaining seven go to online sports betting services providers through public procurement. Each eligible entity may contract with only one platform provider, and entities must give notice of intent within 60 days or be permanently disqualified.

Tax (50-27-150): 27.5% annual privilege tax on adjusted gross income, paid monthly by the services provider. AGI is wagers minus federal excise tax minus winnings paid, including the cash value of merchandise. Negative AGI may be carried forward. The tax is in lieu of other state and local taxes and fees on sports betting operations or proceeds, and it is deposited quarterly into the Georgia Sports Betting Proceeds Trust Fund.

Fees and terms (50-27-130, -131): Type 1 licenses carry a $100,000 application fee and a $1M annual fee. Services provider licenses are $10,000/$100,000, and supplier licenses are $2,000/$20,000. Licenses run five years. Operators must hold a reserve of at least $500,000 or their outstanding wager liabilities, whichever is greater. Operators licensed elsewhere may receive temporary licenses for up to one year.

Launch timing: Lottery rules are due within 90 days, exempt from the Georgia APA. Applications for all 16 licenses open on the same date, and timely applicants get a common go-live date no later than July 31, 2027. No Type 1 licensee may launch until at least one procurement-based provider is licensed.

Wagering scope: bettors must be 21 or older and physically present in Georgia. Wagers covered include in-play, parlay, props and exchange wagering. Proposition bets on collegiate sporting events are banned (50-27-135). Youth events with mostly under-18 participants and Special Olympics are excluded. Official league data is defined for settling tier 2 wagers, but the operative mandate falls in the truncated portion of the text.

Regulatory limits and carve-outs: the corporation may not set hold or payout percentages (50-27-123(b)). Leagues and Type 1 eligible entities may sign revenue-share agreements without corporation approval (50-27-131(d)). Institutional investors are exempt from qualification requirements. The corporation must set responsible gaming rules covering self-exclusion (SSN required), bet limits for problem gamblers, 1-800-GAMBLER notices and advertising guidelines aimed at minors.
GA-HB686.comparison: Like HI HB 2570 and HI HB 1308, HB 686 creates a full licensing regime from scratch. Hawaii places regulation in DBEDT or the Department of Law Enforcement and taxes through a general excise tax on operator licenses. Georgia instead uses its lottery corporation as regulator and operator, with a team- and venue-tethered cap of 16 licenses. Georgia's 27.5% GGR rate sits well above Colorado's 10% rate (whose deductions CO HB 25-1311 narrows) and is in the range of higher-tax states like Louisiana after LA HB 639. Unlike CO SB 131, Georgia leaves deposit and bet limits to rulemaking rather than fixing statutory caps.
GA-HB686.watch: Watch three things: the scarcity of the seven procurement-based skins and the one-platform-per-Type-1-entity rule; the 27.5% rate, where the only promotional relief is the merchandise-as-winnings language in the AGI definition; and the truncated official league data provisions for tier 2 wagers, which could impose data-purchase costs.

IA-SF605.summary: SF 605 amends Iowa Code section 99F.18 to declare that all winnings from sports wagering authorized under chapter 99F are Iowa earned income subject to state and federal income tax, with any state tax withheld remitted to the Department of Revenue on the winner's behalf. It also amends section 422.16(2)(d) to require state income tax withholding on sports wagering winnings whenever federal withholding is required on the same winnings under the Internal Revenue Code. The Act takes effect January 1, 2026.
mechanics: Sec. 1 splits 99F.18 into two subsections: subsection 1 keeps the existing rule for slot machine winnings, and new subsection 2 extends the same earned-income treatment and remittance duty to sports wagering winnings under chapter 99F.

Sec. 2 adds a state withholding trigger for chapter 99F sports wagering that is tied to the federal trigger. State tax must be withheld whenever the Internal Revenue Code requires federal withholding on the same winnings, rather than at a fixed dollar threshold.
Existing state withholding thresholds are unchanged: winnings over $600 under chapters 99B and 99G, over $1,000 under chapter 99D, and over $1,200 for slot machines under chapter 99F.
Operators must remit amounts withheld under 422.16(2) to the Iowa Department of Revenue on behalf of the winner.
Sec. 3 makes the Act effective January 1, 2026. It was signed by the Governor on March 28, 2025.
IA-SF605.comparison: Unlike the operator-side tax measures listed, SF 605 addresses only bettor-level income tax withholding and does not touch the operator tax rate or how it is calculated. Those operator-side measures are LA HB 639, which changes the online sports wagering tax, and CO HB 25-1311, which limits deductions from net sports betting proceeds. It also differs from the comprehensive authorization bills, GA HB 686 and HI HB 1308/HB 2570, which create licensing and tax frameworks from scratch. What is unusual is that Iowa ties state withholding to the federal trigger instead of setting its own dollar threshold, so the state obligation will move automatically with any change to federal withholding rules.
IA-SF605.watch: Operators should update payout and withholding systems before January 1, 2026 so that Iowa withholding is triggered in lockstep with federal withholding on sports wagering winnings. They should also watch for Department of Revenue guidance on the withholding rate, remittance timing, and how federal threshold changes flow through.

LA-SB339.summary: Act 494 gives Louisiana's gaming regulators (the Gaming Control Board and State Police gaming enforcement division, the Racing Commission, the Office of Charitable Gaming, and the Lottery Corporation via the gaming enforcement division) express statutory authority to obtain state and FBI fingerprint-based criminal history record information on applicants, licensees, permittees, and employees. Under the Gaming Control Board's Title 27 jurisdiction, which expressly includes the Louisiana Sports Wagering Act and Fantasy Sports Contests Act, every license or permit applicant and every person required to be found suitable must now submit a full set of fingerprints for a national check. The Act takes effect August 1, 2026.
mechanics: New R.S. 27:15(B)(1)(b) requires every applicant for a license or permit, and any person required to be found suitable under Title 27, to submit fingerprints to the gaming enforcement division, which forwards them to the FBI. The board and the division are the designated recipients of the results.

New R.S. 27:20.1 defines 'criminal history record information' to include state arrest, prosecution, and conviction records, including those expunged or dismissed under Code of Criminal Procedure Articles 893 and 894, plus national fingerprint-based records. The definition of 'permit' covers any permit, license, or authorization, or associated application, issued under Title 27.

Use of fingerprints is limited to eligibility determinations under the suitability standards in R.S. 27:28, 234, 235, 306, 427, and 604. The records are confidential under R.S. 27:21 and may be used exclusively to evaluate eligibility or disqualification. They are also available to the board and the Louisiana Department of Justice.

The bureau's costs under R.S. 15:587, including the costs of the FBI check, may be imposed on the individual. Under amended R.S. 47:9065(B), the bureau may charge the Lottery Corporation or the applicant a reasonable processing fee.

Parallel sections are added for the Racing Commission (R.S. 4:147.3, tied to R.S. 4:150 suitability) and the Office of Charitable Gaming (R.S. 4:705.1). R.S. 15:587(C) is rewritten to route state and FBI results to each agency.
Under new R.S. 47:9065(C), the gaming enforcement division may share criminal history results with the Lottery Corporation to determine eligibility of vendors, retailers, and employees.
LA-SB339.comparison: No other states' bills were listed for comparison. On its own, the Act is unusual in two respects. It is a cross-agency housekeeping statute that recodifies express FBI fingerprint-check authority for every Louisiana gaming regulator at once. It also explicitly sweeps expunged and Article 893/894 dismissed records into what regulators may review, rather than changing any substantive licensing standard, tax, or operating rule.
LA-SB339.watch: Operators should watch how the board applies the new mandatory fingerprinting of 'any person required to be found suitable', which could extend to key persons, owners, vendors, and employees of sports wagering and fantasy licensees, along with the review of expunged or dismissed records and the pass-through of check fees to individuals.

IA-SSB1152.summary: Iowa SSB 1152, a Department of Revenue bill later renumbered SF 605, amends Code section 99F.18 to declare that all winnings from sports wagering authorized under chapter 99F are Iowa earned income subject to state and federal income tax. It amends section 422.16(2)(d) to require Iowa income tax withholding on sports wagering winnings whenever federal withholding is required on the same winnings under the Internal Revenue Code. Amounts withheld must be remitted to the Department of Revenue on the winner's behalf.
mechanics: Sec. 1 adds new subsection 2 to Iowa Code 99F.18. It states that all sports wagering winnings under chapter 99F are Iowa earned income subject to state and federal income tax laws.

Sec. 1 also requires that amounts deducted from sports wagering winnings under 422.16(2) be remitted to the Department of Revenue on behalf of the winner, mirroring the existing slot machine rule in 99F.18(1).

Sec. 2 amends 422.16(2)(d) to tie the state withholding trigger for sports wagering to the federal trigger. Under IRC rules this is generally winnings over $5,000 that are at least 300 times the wager.
The existing withholding thresholds stay the same: $600 for chapter 99B and 99G (lottery) winnings, $1,000 for chapter 99D (pari-mutuel) winnings, and $1,200 for chapter 99F slot machines.
The bill sets no state withholding rate; the rate is governed by existing 422.16.
Sec. 3 makes the Act effective January 1, 2026.
IA-SSB1152.comparison: Unlike CO HB 25-1311 and LA HB 639, which change operator-level taxes on net sports betting proceeds or online wagering, Iowa SSB 1152 targets only patron-level income tax withholding and leaves operators' gaming tax untouched. It is also far narrower than the framework bills in GA HB 686, HI HB 1308 and HI HB 2570, which authorize, license and tax sports wagering wholesale. Its distinguishing feature is that it ties the state withholding trigger to federal rules rather than setting a fixed dollar threshold, as Iowa does for slots, lottery and pari-mutuel winnings.
IA-SSB1152.watch: Operators should prepare payment and withholding systems so that, from January 1, 2026, Iowa withholding fires automatically on every sports wagering payout that triggers federal withholding (including after any future federal threshold changes), with remittance to the Department of Revenue handled as for slot winnings.

IA-HSB91.summary: Iowa HSB 91, a Department of Revenue proposal later renumbered HF 794, amends Iowa Code section 99F.18 to declare that all winnings from sports wagering authorized under chapter 99F are Iowa earned income subject to state and federal income tax. It also amends section 422.16(2)(d) to require Iowa income tax withholding on sports wagering winnings whenever federal withholding is required on the same winnings under the Internal Revenue Code. The Act takes effect January 1, 2026.
mechanics: Sec. 1 adds new subsection 2 to section 99F.18 (Tax on winnings). All winnings from chapter 99F sports wagering are Iowa earned income, and amounts deducted for state tax under section 422.16(2) must be remitted to the Department of Revenue on the winner's behalf.

Sec. 2 amends section 422.16(2)(d) to tie the state withholding trigger for sports wagering to the federal trigger: withhold state tax whenever federal income tax withholding is required on the same winnings under the IRC.
Covered parties are sports wagering licensees and operators under chapter 99F that pay out winnings subject to federal withholding.
Sec. 3 sets the effective date as January 1, 2026.
IA-HSB91.comparison: Unlike CO HB 25-1311 and LA HB 639, which change operator-level taxes, HSB 91 targets bettor income tax withholding. CO HB 25-1311 changes deductions from net sports betting proceeds, and LA HB 639 changes online sports wagering tax rates and dedications. HSB 91 leaves the operator tax untouched and instead imposes a payout-side compliance duty on operators. Also unlike GA HB 686 and HI HB 2570/HB 1308, which would create new sports betting regimes with licensing and gross revenue or excise taxes, Iowa's bill is a narrow administrative fix by the revenue department within an existing legal market. Its most unusual feature is that it sets no fixed dollar threshold for state withholding and instead conforms automatically to the federal withholding trigger.
IA-HSB91.watch: Operators should map their payout and withholding systems to the federal IRC withholding rules before January 1, 2026, since the bill sets no fixed dollar threshold. Any future federal change to sports wagering withholding (for example, the trigger amount or the 300-to-1 odds test) would automatically change Iowa withholding obligations.

HI-HB2570.summary: HB 2570 HD1 (the "Representative Daniel Holt Act") adds a new HRS chapter legalizing mobile-only sports wagering in Hawaii, regulated and licensed by the Department of Business, Economic Development, and Tourism, with at least six operator licenses and a universal launch date. It taxes operators through a new privilege tax under amended HRS §237-13(9), earmarks revenue to UH Manoa athletics, a Native Hawaiian organization, an AFL-CIO affiliate, the general fund, problem gambling, and education, and creates escalating criminal penalties for unlicensed wagering. It also expressly exempts licensed sports wagering and defined fantasy sports contests from the gambling offenses in HRS ch. 712 part III.
mechanics: Licensing (§-5, §-6): DBEDT must issue a minimum of six sports wagering operator licenses, open only to a "qualified gaming entity"; $500,000 initial/renewal fee plus cost-based processing fees; five-year term; temporary licenses valid up to three years on payment of the initial fee; universal start date no later than 180 days after the Act's effective date, with equal launch for entities applying within 30 days of the application window. Supplier licenses cost $10,000 for five years, and DBEDT may accept approvals from other jurisdictions with similar standards.

Scope and wagers (§-1, §-10): mobile or digital platform only, with no kiosks or terminals at physical locations; bettors must be 21 or older and physically in Hawaii unless an interstate or international agreement under §-9 applies. Pro, collegiate, amateur, Olympic, motorsports and e-sports are covered. Youth events are excluded, as are games involving Hawaii-based colleges, including those teams' individual games within tournaments. Layoff wagers are permitted, and accounts may be funded by card, bank transfer, online payment systems, or bonuses and promotions.

Tax (§-12, §237-13(9)): operators pay the §237-13(9) privilege tax on adjusted gross sports wagering receipts using accrual accounting, in lieu of all other taxes on sports wagering. Adjusted gross receipts are gross receipts less winnings and applicable taxes, including federal excise tax, with no promotional deduction. The rate text in §237-13(9) is not in the excerpt provided. §-12(a) allocates 2% to UH Manoa athletics, 2% to a Native Hawaiian organization, 1% to the Hawaii Employees Lifeline Program (an AFL-CIO affiliate) and 10% to the general fund. §-12(b) separately directs 7% of all taxes to a new DOH problem gambling special fund (§-13) and 7% to education.

Mandatory rulemaking (§-2(f)) covers: geolocation, age and identity verification; integrity and AML; data privacy and cybersecurity; a statewide voluntary exclusion program; patron-set limits on wagers, deposits and time; and advertising rules barring targeting of minors and self-excluded persons. Rules must also prohibit bets on injuries, penalties, player discipline rulings, replay reviews and any other bet type harmful to an athlete or patron. Rules are to be consistent with other jurisdictions where commercially reasonable.

Operator duties (§-7, §-8, §-11): operators need department-approved house rules. They must run suspicious-activity monitoring software, report suspicious betting above an operator-set, department-approved threshold, and display 1-800-GAMBLER in all advertising. They must keep daily records of gross and adjusted gross receipts and honor the exclusion list, which is distributed at least quarterly.

Enforcement (§-4, §-14, §-15): civil fines of up to $5,000 per violation or $10,000 per occurrence, applicable to non-licensees. Unlicensed sports wagering is a misdemeanor with a minimum $10,000 fine for a first offense, a class C felony with a minimum $50,000 fine for a second, and a class B felony with a minimum $100,000 fine for a third or later. Control persons for background checks are 15% owners with control, parents and subsidiaries, and key decision-makers.
HI-HB2570.comparison: Like GA HB 686, this is a full legalization-and-tax framework, but Hawaii is mobile-only, bans retail kiosks entirely and sets a floor of six licenses rather than a cap. Unlike KS SB 356, which only authorizes regulations for an existing Kansas market, or CO SB 131, which imposes specific statutory deposit caps, Hawaii leaves responsible-gaming limits and bans on certain prop and bet types to DBEDT rulemaking. On tax base, Hawaii's adjusted gross receipts deduct only winnings and taxes, with no promotional-credit deduction, which goes further than the deduction narrowing at issue in CO HB 25-1311. Its escalating felony penalties for unlicensed operators parallel AR HB 1861's approach.
HI-HB2570.watch: Watch the actual §237-13(9) rate, which is absent from this excerpt, and the internally inconsistent revenue allocations in §-12(a) and (b), along with the undefined "qualified gaming entity" eligibility standard and the rule-delegated bans on injury, penalty and replay bets that could narrow the prop menu as the bill moves through JHA and CPC.

IA-HSB330.summary: HSB 330 (renumbered HF 1041) rewrites how Iowa spends money in the sports wagering receipts fund (Code 8.57I), which is fed by the sports wagering net receipts tax (99F.11(5)) and the internet fantasy sports contest tax (99E.6). Starting FY 2025-26 it sets a standing priority list of appropriations. It also makes three $10 million one-time FY 2024-25 appropriations from the fund. It does not change tax rates, licensing or any operator obligations.
mechanics: Sec. 2 replaces 8.57I(4)-(5) for FY 2025-26 onward with an ordered list paid from each year's deposits: first $1.75M to HHS for behavioral health and problem gambling prevention, treatment and recovery; next $750,000 to the Economic Development Authority, split equally among regional sports authority districts (15E.321); next $1.5M to the Department of Revenue's length of service award program grant fund (100B.52).

Under Sec. 2, the remainder is split 50% to the public safety equipment fund (80.48) and 50% to a new local emergency services equipment grant account run by the Department of Management. Eligible grantees are the 88 least populous counties and small cities as defined in 15.352, and DOM must adopt rules under chapter 17A.
Under Sec. 6, the $1.5M length of service award program allocation takes effect only if HF 1002 or SF 627 (or successor legislation) is enacted.

Sec. 4 appropriates from the fund for FY 2024-25: $10M to the community attraction and tourism fund, $10M to the Destination Iowa fund and $10M to the levee improvement fund. Sec. 5 makes this effective on enactment.

According to the explanation, Secs. 1 and 3 strike three things: the authority to use fund moneys for cash flow, the project reporting requirements, and the requirement that county endowment grantees consider racetrack-operating charities when using sports wagering money (no such transfers occur under current law).
IA-HSB330.comparison: No other states' bills are listed for comparison. What is unusual is that the bill deals only with where existing sports wagering and fantasy sports tax revenue goes, not with the rate or base. It also earmarks most of the residual revenue for public safety and rural emergency equipment rather than the general fund or education.
IA-HSB330.watch: The bill leaves rates untouched, but operators should watch HF 1041 for amendments, because tying sports wagering receipts to public safety and rural emergency grants creates constituencies that may later push for higher net receipts tax rates or a broader tax base to grow the 50/50 residual pool.

AZ-HB2592.summary: HB 2592 is an omnibus tax-base broadening bill that repeals selected Arizona tax exemptions. For gaming, Section 1 amends A.R.S. 5-111(C) so that the state's pari-mutuel percentage, which previously did not apply to wagering on simulcasts of out-of-state races, now also applies to those pools. The rest of the visible text repeals transaction privilege tax retail exemptions for warranty and service contracts and for sales of stocks and bonds, with conforming renumbering across Titles 28 and 42.
mechanics: Sec. 1, A.R.S. 5-111(C): the state's take of 2% of the first $1,000,000 of daily pari-mutuel pools and 5% of the amount above $1,000,000 is extended to pools on simulcasts of out-of-state races, repealing the existing carve-out.

The existing 5-111 exemptions are retained in the shown text: county fair racing meetings (D), charity racing days (E), unclaimed tickets from unclaimed property law (F), and permittee pari-mutuel receipts and purse monies from Title 42, Chapter 5 TPT (G).

Sec. 5, A.R.S. 42-5061(A): repeals the retail TPT exclusions for sales of warranty or service contracts (former para. 3) and for the sale of stocks and bonds (former para. 7), and renumbers the remaining paragraphs.
Secs. 2-4 (28-2154.01, 42-5008.01, 42-5009) make conforming cross-reference changes to reflect the renumbering.
The title also lists amendments to 42-5071, 42-5072, 42-5075, 42-6017 and 43-1111, but those sections fall outside the supplied text, which is truncated at 42-5061(A)(34).
No effective date or enforcement provision appears in the supplied text. Status: second reading in the House on 2025-01-28.
AZ-HB2592.comparison: Unlike LA HB 639 (online sports wagering tax changes) and CO HB 25-1311 (limits on operator deductions from net sports betting proceeds), HB 2592 does not touch Arizona's event wagering tax. Its gaming hook is narrower: removing a pari-mutuel simulcast exemption for horse racing. It also differs from the IA withholding bills (SF 605, SSB 1152, HSB 91), which target bettor winnings rather than operator or permittee liability. What is unusual is that a gaming tax increase is folded into a general exemption-repeal bill instead of a standalone gaming measure.
AZ-HB2592.watch: Watch whether this exemption-repeal approach widens in amendment to reach event wagering deductions or other Title 5 carve-outs, and how much extending the state's 2% to 5% take to out-of-state simulcast pools would raise costs for racetrack permittees and the advance-deposit or simulcast wagering clients.

LA-SB325.summary: Act 491 amends R.S. 27:27.2 to require the Louisiana Gaming Control Board to adopt rules creating a separate exclusion list for retail sports books and mobile wagering, covering people already on the general gaming exclusion list, people who threaten violence or harm against anyone involved in a sporting event where the threat relates to sports gaming, and anyone the board finds threatens the state's interests or effective sports wagering regulation. It makes clear that both the board and the division can place people on exclusion lists, bars listing based on race, color, creed, national origin, sex or disability, and re-letters the existing notice, petition, penalty, sanction and hearing provisions. Effective August 1, 2026.
mechanics: New R.S. 27:27.2(B): the board must adopt rules for a list of persons to be excluded or ejected from retail sports books and barred from the play or operation of mobile wagering under a license or contract issued under Title 27.

Three listing categories under (B): (1) persons excluded under Subsection A; (2) persons who, before, during or after a sporting event, threaten violence or harm against any person involved in the event, where the threat is related to sports gaming; (3) persons the board determines pose a threat to the state's interests, the purposes of Title 27, or the strict and effective regulation of sports wagering.
New (C): the board and the division may both place persons on the list, but not because of race, color, creed, national origin, sex or disability (as defined in R.S. 51:2232).

Carried-over provisions, re-lettered: notice by personal service or certified mail (D); a petition for removal, where the petitioner bears the burden of proof (E); entering or attempting to enter after listing is punishable by up to 6 months' imprisonment and/or a fine of up to $500 (F); and a hearing within 30 days of the petition under R.S. 27:25 (H).

Operator exposure under (G): the board may sanction licensees, permittees or the casino operator for willful failure to exclude a listed person, and may seek suspension or revocation for a pattern of willful failure.
Effective August 1, 2026, as Act No. 491. Video draw poker licensees remain exempt under (I).
LA-SB325.comparison: No comparable bills from other states were listed. The unusual feature is that it ties exclusion from sports wagering, including mobile accounts, to threats of violence against athletes, officials or others involved in a sporting event when the threat is linked to betting. That targets bettor harassment rather than the traditional casino exclusion grounds such as cheating or criminal history. The catch-all in (B)(3) gives the board broad discretion to exclude anyone it deems a threat to effective sports wagering regulation.
LA-SB325.watch: Watch the board's implementing rules for how mobile operators must identify, block and eject listed persons, and how 'willful failure to exclude' under Section 27.2(G) will be applied to online accounts, because that failure is a basis for sanctions and, if it forms a pattern, license suspension or revocation.

LA-HB513.summary: Act 810 rewrites Louisiana's college NIL statute (R.S. 17:3701 et seq.) and, in new R.S. 17:3705, extends NIL rights to high school athletes for the first time. The high school provisions ban NIL compensation tied to a list of restricted categories that includes gaming, gambling, or wagering, expressly including sports wagering. The college provisions update agent rules, raise disclosure obligations to a $600 threshold, broaden institutional liability shields, and require management-board NIL policies.
mechanics: New R.S. 17:3705(E)(2)(d) bars interscholastic athletes (students in grades 9-12 at public or nonpublic high schools) from earning NIL compensation in connection with "gaming, gambling, or wagering, including but not limited to sports wagering." The same list covers alcohol, cannabis, adult entertainment, tobacco and vapor products, weapons, and performance-enhancing drugs.

Under 3705(B), NIL agreements signed by high school athletes under 18 are valid only with written parental or guardian consent. Under 3705(G), athletes must disclose proposed agreements to the school before signing, and under 3705(J) an aggrieved athlete may sue for injunctive relief.

High schools and athletic associations may not bar NIL earnings or representation, or declare an athlete ineligible for engaging in them (3705(C)-(D)). Schools may still restrict NIL activity during team or academic activities, block deals that conflict with existing school agreements, and control use of school marks (3705(F)).
Under R.S. 17:3703(I), college athletes must disclose NIL contracts worth $600 or more to their institution, with reporting rules aligned to the applicable athletic governing commission.

R.S. 17:3703(D) requires athlete agents to be registered under R.S. 4:422 and comply with the federal SPARTA. Section 3703(L) shields institutions, affiliated nonprofits, and staff from liability over third-party NIL deals, except for gross negligence or intentional misconduct.

Section 3703(N) requires management boards to adopt NIL policies covering compensation, institutional involvement, use of marks, representation, education, enforcement, and a compliance contact. Institutions cannot implement the Chapter until their board acts.
LA-HB513.comparison: Like HI HB 2384 and KY SB 3, LA HB 513 adapts state NIL law to the post-settlement institutional-agreement era, with board-adopted policies and disclosure requirements. Unlike either of those, it extends NIL rights to high school athletes and expressly bars minors' NIL deals involving sports wagering. KY HB 904 is a gaming-regulation bill on fantasy contests and is not comparable in substance. The only overlap is that both touch on who may be marketed to or associated with wagering products.
LA-HB513.watch: Operators and their marketing affiliates should screen influencer and endorsement programs to exclude Louisiana high school athletes under R.S. 17:3705(E)(2)(d). Note that this Act imposes no comparable gaming ban on college athletes, so any restrictions there come from LGCB advertising rules and institutional policies.

HI-HB2384.summary: HB 2384 HD2 adds a new subpart to HRS chapter 304A creating a name, image, and likeness (NIL) framework for University of Hawaii student-athletes. It affirms their right to earn NIL compensation, requires the university to adopt NIL, disclosure, agent, education, and Title IX policies, and requires annual aggregate reporting to the legislature. Its only gaming link is that the university may bar student-athletes from NIL deals involving gambling or sports wagering.
mechanics: New §304A-(c)(3) lets the university prohibit NIL agreements involving "gambling, sports wagering, or illegal drugs," alongside adult entertainment, firearms, tobacco/vaping, and any industry that conflicts with the university's mission or financial interests.

Student-athletes must disclose third-party NIL deals worth $600 or more, or an alternative threshold set by NCAA rules or federal law. They may rescind any institutional or third-party NIL agreement within at least ten business days of signing.

The university, conferences, and the NCAA may not unduly restrict NIL activity, except to comply with law, post-House settlement governing-body rules, or reasonable, neutral policies on conflicts of interest, time commitments, or prohibited industries.

Annual reports to the legislature begin with the 2028 session and cover state-funded institutional NIL spending by team and gender, compliance measures, and violations. Underlying records are exempt from chapter 92F disclosure.
Section 3 makes a general-fund appropriation for FY2026-27, with the amount left blank, including for direct institutional NIL payments.
Section 5 sets a placeholder effective date of July 1, 3000, a sunset of June 30, 2030, and a planned legislative review in the 2029 session.
HI-HB2384.comparison: Like KY SB 3 and LA HB 513, this is a student-athlete NIL bill updating state law after the House v. NCAA settlement. Hawaii's version is limited to the University of Hawaii, whereas LA HB 513 also reaches interscholastic athletes. Unlike KY HB 904, which directly regulates gaming (fantasy contest operators, geolocation), HB 2384 touches wagering only through a permissive prohibited-industries list for NIL endorsements. Its defective 3000 effective date and blank appropriation signal it is still a vehicle for conference negotiation.
HI-HB2384.watch: Watch whether the permissive gambling and sports-wagering NIL exclusion in §304A-(c)(3) is hardened into a mandatory ban, or broadened, as the bill moves through EDU and WAM/CPN, since that would limit operator sponsorship and endorsement deals with UH athletes if Hawaii ever authorizes wagering.

HI-HB1308.summary: HB 1308 HD3 SD2 would legalize mobile-only sports wagering in Hawaii under a new HRS chapter regulated by the Department of Law Enforcement, with at least four operator licenses limited to qualified gaming entities and a separate supplier license. It taxes licensees at 10% of adjusted gross sports wagering receipts through a new general excise tax paragraph, section 237-13(9), in lieu of all other taxes on sports wagering, and earmarks part of that revenue for problem gambling and education. It also creates misdemeanor and felony penalties for unlicensed sports wagering and amends the chapter 712 gambling definitions (the supplied text cuts off in Section 3).
mechanics: Licensing: the Department of Law Enforcement must issue a minimum of four operator licenses (§-5), open only to a 'qualified gaming entity', meaning one already offering online sports wagering in Hawaii or in at least three US jurisdictions. The fee is $250,000 per five-year term plus cost-based processing fees. Supplier licenses cost $10,000 per five-year term. Three-year temporary licenses are available on payment of the initial fee. A universal start date must be set no later than 180 days after the effective date.

Tax: 10% of adjusted gross sports wagering receipts under new §237-13(9), which by its terms applies to both licensed operators and suppliers, on the accrual method. The receipts base is gross wagers less winnings paid, with no express deduction for promotional credits. Of collections, 7% goes to a DOH-run problem gambling special fund and 7% to education programs (§-11, §-12).

Wagering scope: mobile or digital platforms only, with no kiosks or retail terminals. Bettors must be 21 or older and physically in Hawaii unless the department signs an interstate or international agreement (§-9). Covered events include professional, collegiate (with no in-state college carve-out), amateur, Olympic, motorsports and e-sports. Youth events are excluded. Props, in-play, parlays, pools and exchange wagering are expressly included, and fantasy contests are excluded.

Operator duties (§-8, §-10): integrity monitoring for volume and odds irregularities, with reporting to the department; suspicious-bet reporting above an operator-set, department-approved threshold; department-approved house rules; '1-800-GAMBLER' in all advertising; daily receipts records; and an employee betting ban. Layoff wagers between operators are allowed. Accounts may be funded by card, bonuses or promotions, bank transfer or e-wallet.

Responsible gaming: a department-run voluntary self-exclusion program of up to lifetime duration. Operators must make reasonable efforts to stop direct marketing to excluded persons, may share the exclusion list with out-of-state affiliates, and receive the list at least quarterly.

Enforcement: civil fines up to $5,000 per violation or $10,000 per occurrence, applicable to non-licensees (§-13). Unlicensed wagering is a misdemeanor with a fine of at least $10,000 on a first offense, a class C felony with at least $50,000 on a second, and a class B felony with at least $100,000 on a third or later offense (§-14).
HI-HB1308.comparison: Like GA HB 686, this is a ground-up legalization act, but Hawaii's version is mobile-only with no retail or tribal/casino tether. It sets a license floor rather than a cap, and access is gated by prior multi-state operating experience. Its 10% rate matches the Colorado rate referenced in CO HB 25-1311, but Hawaii's base already allows deduction only of winnings paid, avoiding the promotional-deduction fight in Colorado. It is well below the rate-hike direction in LA HB 639. Unlike AR HB 1861, which focuses on criminalizing illegal online operators, Hawaii pairs legalization with an escalating felony ladder. It also lacks the deposit-frequency and other consumer-protection limits in CO SB 131.
HI-HB1308.watch: Watch whether the bill survives conference after the discharge of House conferees, and whether the drafting that extends the 10% tax to suppliers and the generic 'subject to federal income tax' winnings deduction are fixed. Also watch the department's rulemaking on temporary licenses, the tight 180-day universal start date and the operator-set suspicious-bet threshold.

CO-SB163.summary: Colorado SB 163 is a regulatory clean-up and enforcement bill for the Limited Gaming Act of 1991 and sports betting law. It lets the Limited Gaming Control Commission delegate more licensing duties to the Division of Gaming, authorizes division investigators to inspect and impound premises suspected of unlicensed gaming or sports betting, and extends the voluntary self-exclusion program to sports betting. It also moves game pre-approval from the commission to the division and clarifies the fingerprint-based background check process.
mechanics: The commission may delegate to the Division of Gaming licensing duties found anywhere in the gaming act, not only the specific duties currently listed.
Division investigators and their supervisors may inspect, examine, investigate, hold, or impound any premises in Colorado where they suspect unlicensed gaming or unlicensed sports betting.
The division's voluntary self-exclusion program, which currently covers gaming, is expanded to cover sports betting.
A designee of the director is a peace officer while performing their duties, with primary authority that includes enforcing all state laws.
Licensees need prior approval from the division, rather than the commission, before offering certain games.

The bill clarifies the definition of 'race meet', adds other gaming definitions, and clarifies how the commission and the Colorado Bureau of Investigation run fingerprint-based background checks on license applicants. Full text was unavailable, so the specific statutory sections and effective date could not be confirmed.
CO-SB163.comparison: Unlike the authorization and tax bills on the list (GA HB 686, HI HB 2570 and HB 1308, LA HB 639, IA SF 613 and SSB 1157), CO SB 163 does not touch tax rates or market structure; it is administrative and enforcement housekeeping for an existing market. Its enforcement against unlicensed operators parallels AR HB 1861, which makes operating an illegal online casino or sportsbook a felony, though Colorado uses administrative inspection and impoundment rather than new criminal penalties. Its shift of authority from commission to agency resembles Kentucky's HB 566 corporation clean-up and Kansas SB 356's grant of rulemaking authority to the racing and gaming commission.
CO-SB163.watch: Operators should watch for division rulemaking that sets up the sports-betting self-exclusion program, including how exclusion lists are shared with operators, compliance obligations, and liability for serving excluded patrons, along with any faster or stricter game-approval process now that the division, not the commission, grants approval.

KY-HB757.summary: HB 757 is Kentucky's 2026 omnibus revenue bill, enacted with an emergency clause as Acts Ch. 161. It updates Kentucky's Internal Revenue Code conformity date to December 31, 2025, decouples from several new federal individual deductions, simplifies the marketplace-provider sales tax nexus test, sunsets the state's three tax increment financing participation programs, and makes technical changes to tax interest and TVA payment reporting. In the portion of the text provided, it does not amend Kentucky's sports wagering licensing or tax provisions.
mechanics: Section 1 (KRS 139.450): the marketplace-provider collection obligation is triggered only by more than $100,000 in sales. The 200-transaction alternative threshold is deleted, and services provided to Kentucky purchasers are expressly covered.
Section 6 (KRS 141.010(21)): for taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2026, the Internal Revenue Code is adopted as in effect on December 31, 2025.

Section 7 (KRS 141.019(2)): Kentucky still disallows federal itemized loss deductions under 26 U.S.C. 165 except wagering losses allowed under Section 165(d). Because of the updated conformity date, that carve-out now follows whatever 165(d) says as of December 31, 2025.

Section 7 also decouples from the new federal deductions for qualified tips (sec. 224), overtime (sec. 225) and passenger vehicle loan interest (sec. 163(h)(4)), and from sec. 174A R&E expensing. It limits mortgage interest to acquisition debt on one principal residence for 2026 and later.

Section 5 (KRS 154.30-030): all three state TIF participation programs sunset on the section's effective date. No new applications or amendments to existing agreements are allowed, and previously approved projects are grandfathered.

Section 2 (KRS 131.183): obsolete 2008 transition language is deleted, keeping prime plus 2% on underpayments and prime minus 2% on overpayments. Section 4 redirects TVA regional development agency reports to the Department for Local Government, which must report to the LRC by December 1.
KY-HB757.comparison: Iowa's SF 605, SSB 1152 and HSB 91 address state withholding on sports wagering winnings, and Colorado HB 25-1311 and Louisiana HB 639 change operator-level deductions and tax rates. Kentucky HB 757 does none of these, at least in the text provided. Its only gaming touchpoint is the existing individual income tax carve-out for wagering losses under IRC 165(d), now tied to a 2025 federal code. That makes it closer in character to the general tax omnibus bills such as Florida HB 7031 or Arizona SB 1274 than to Georgia HB 686 or Hawaii HB 2570, which are full sports-betting authorization bills.
KY-HB757.watch: The supplied text is cut off partway through Section 8, so check the remaining sections for any changes to Kentucky's wagering excise tax or withholding rules, and confirm whether rolling conformity to the December 31, 2025 IRC imports the federal change limiting 165(d) wagering-loss deductions for Kentucky bettors.

KY-HB904.summary: HB 904 (Acts Ch. 184) creates a licensing regime for paid fantasy contests under the Kentucky Horse Racing and Gaming Corporation, adds fixed-odds wagering on live horse racing to the KRS 138.552 excise tax, and requires licensed online gaming, sports wagering and fantasy operators to block and suspend accounts of people on a child support arrearage registry. It also adds definitions of "event contract" and "prediction market" to KRS 230.210, and lets the Lottery Corporation and the Corporation issue regulations without the Governor's signature. The supplied text is truncated partway through Section 14, so any operative provisions using the new prediction-market definitions are not visible here.
mechanics: Fixed-odds horse racing tax (Section 13, amending KRS 138.552): fixed-odds wagers on live horse racing, and parlays containing one, are taxed at the same rates as sports wagering, 9.75% at the track and 14.25% online. These wagers are carved out of adjusted gross sports wagering revenue. The proceeds go to a new purse stabilization fund (Section 12), which must be held at least 1.5 years and can be spent only to supplement live-meet purses, capped at 10% of the fund.

Fantasy contest licensing (Sections 4-11): providers must be licensed and use geolocation, and players must be 18 or older. Fees (Section 10) are: $7,500 initial and $5,000 renewal for providers already licensed as sports wagering service providers; $15,000 and $10,000 for others; $5,000 and $1,000 for providers under $50,000 in adjusted gross fantasy receipts. Existing operators may keep operating if they apply within 90 days of the regulations, which are due within 180 days. Annual CPA audit and compliance testing are required, deferred 24 months for new licensees (Section 7).

Child support registry (Section 3): the Attorney General compiles a registry of people with arrearages of $500 or more per Title IV-D case, and the Corporation passes it to operators monthly. Operators must screen applicants before opening an account and suspend matching existing accounts within 5 business days, with reinstatement within 5 business days of clearance. Knowing violations can lead to license suspension or revocation, and there is a good-faith safe harbor from private suits. Charitable gaming is exempt.

Integrity (Sections 1, 5, 8, 9): new definitions of prohibited and restricted participants (players, coaches, officials, their family members, and owners of more than 5% of a team), plus a fantasy-tampering offense. Providers must notify the Corporation of match fixing, governing-body rule breaches and illegal activity. The Corporation must investigate allegations and refer credible ones to law enforcement and sports governing bodies.

Definitions (Section 1): adds "event contract" (keyed to CEA 7 U.S.C. 1a(19)(i)), "prediction market" (any platform for event contracts or speculative positions on future events, in or out of state, including a CFTC designated contract market) and "fixed-odds wagering." It removes the horse racing exclusion from the chapter 230 definition of "sporting event" but keeps it in the tax-specific definition.

Responsible gaming and rulemaking (Sections 2, 4, 11): fantasy self-exclusion is folded into the existing program, winnings of self-excluded players are forfeited to problem-gaming charities, and a help statement is required on all marketing. Regulations no longer need the Governor's signature (new KRS Chapter 13A section), and the Corporation may not restrict fantasy contests merely by labeling them sports wagering.
KY-HB904.comparison: Unlike LA HB 639, which raises online sports wagering taxes, and CO HB 25-1311, which narrows operators' deductions, KY HB 904 leaves Kentucky's 9.75%/14.25% rates unchanged and instead applies them to a new product, fixed-odds horse racing, with that revenue reserved for purses. Its prediction-market treatment is definitional (at least in the visible text), whereas IA SF 2085 imposes a permit and a tax on event-contract markets. Its child support arrearage screening and suspension mandate for online operators has no counterpart among the listed bills, such as CO SB 131's deposit limits or the HI sports wagering bills (HB 1308, HB 2570).
KY-HB904.watch: Operators should build monthly child-support registry screening with 5-business-day suspension and reinstatement (knowing violations put the license at risk). They should also check how the new prediction-market and event-contract definitions are used in the untruncated remainder of the Act, since the CFTC-DCM language suggests the Corporation may assert jurisdiction over competing event-contract platforms.

LA-SR178.summary: Louisiana Senate Resolution 178 urges and requests the Louisiana Department of Health to study how to modernize the state's problem gambling prevention and education efforts, with a focus on youth, college-age populations and young adults. It is a non-binding simple resolution: it creates no regulatory obligations, but it asks LDH to deliver a written report with findings and recommendations by February 1, 2027.
mechanics: LDH is urged to study age-appropriate educational resources and curriculum covering gambling-related harms, financial literacy, decision-making, online gaming environments and responsible behavior.
LDH is urged to examine voluntary digital tools and mobile resources for prevention, self-assessment, awareness, early intervention and connection to behavioral health and recovery services.
LDH is to consult with the Department of Education, the Board of Regents, colleges and universities, behavioral health providers, community organizations, researchers and other stakeholders.
A written report is due to the Senate and the David R. Poynter Legislative Research Library under R.S. 24:771 and 772 no later than February 1, 2027.
There are no taxes, fees, operator mandates or enforcement provisions; the whereas clauses cite expanded legal sports wagering and youth exposure through advertising, social media and mobile apps.
LA-SR178.comparison: Unlike the Hawaii sports wagering bills (HB 2570 and HB 1308), SR 178 does not legalize anything or impose any tax. Those bills would create licensing regimes and a Problem Gambling fund, while this resolution only commissions a study. It is also far softer than Colorado SB 131, which imposes direct operator limits such as a cap of 6 deposits per gaming day. SR 178 addresses problem gambling purely through public-health education and voluntary tools, and it places no obligations on licensees.
LA-SR178.watch: Watch the February 1, 2027 LDH report for recommendations that could later become legislation, such as youth-focused advertising restrictions, mandated operator funding for prevention programs or required integration with self-assessment and referral tools.

LA-SB135.summary: SB 135 amends R.S. 27:625(G)(2) and (8) to change how the state treasurer distributes Louisiana's tax on sports wagering net gaming proceeds collected under Subsection B between two dedicated funds. As engrossed, both provisions credit 25% of Subsection B collections, capped at $20 million, to the Louisiana Early Childhood Education Fund (R.S. 17:407.30) and to the Supporting Programs, Opportunities, Resources, and Teams (SPORT) Fund (R.S. 17:1792). It does not change the tax rate or any operator obligation.
mechanics: Amends R.S. 27:625(G)(2): 25% of Subsection B collections, 'not to exceed twenty million dollars,' goes to the Louisiana Early Childhood Education Fund. The digest describes this as tied to net mobile sports wagering proceeds.
Amends R.S. 27:625(G)(8): adds a $20 million cap on the 25% share of Subsection B collections credited to the SPORT Fund, which was previously uncapped per the digest.
Distributions apply each fiscal year only after the Subsection D requirements are met.
Senate Finance amendments dropped an earlier version that guaranteed the Early Childhood fund the greater of 25% or $20 million, removing that floor.
Effective July 1, 2027, moved from July 1, 2026 by committee amendment. Passed the Senate and on 2026-05-18 was referred to the House Committee on Administration of Criminal Justice.
LA-SB135.comparison: No comparable bills from other states are listed. This bill is unusual because it only reallocates already-collected sports wagering tax revenue between two education and youth funds, with no change to rates, licensing or conduct rules. The digest also conflicts with the bill text: it says the $20 million cap on the Early Childhood fund is removed, yet the visible engrossed text keeps the cap. The lost strikethrough formatting makes the final effect on that fund uncertain.
LA-SB135.watch: The bill does not touch operator tax rates as engrossed, but in the House it is a vehicle on R.S. 27:625, so watch for amendments that raise the Subsection B rate or change the deductions behind net gaming proceeds to fund these capped dedications.

IA-SF660.summary: SF 660 does not change how sports wagering is taxed, licensed or conducted in Iowa; it spends money from the sports wagering receipts fund (Iowa Code 8.57I). It adds two ongoing claims on the fund and four one-time FY2025-26 appropriations. It also creates a new Iowa major events and tourism grant program (new chapter 15G) and repeals the sports tourism marketing fund (15F.403), moving that fund's balance into the new program.
mechanics: Sec. 1 amends 8.57I(3) to make a standing annual appropriation of $8 million from the sports wagering receipts fund to the public safety equipment fund (80.48), starting FY2025-26, exempt from the reporting rules in subsections 4 and 5.

Sec. 2 adds 8.57I(3A): from FY2026-27, the fund must top up the length of service award program grant fund (100B.52) to a $1.5 million balance each July 1. This takes effect only if HF 1002 is enacted (Sec. 8) and is repealed July 1, 2030.

Secs. 3-6 make one-time FY2025-26 appropriations from the fund: $14 million for education support personnel pay, split among school districts by budget enrollment and effective on enactment (Sec. 7); $5 million for the special education division; $4 million to the film production incentive fund, contingent on SF 657; and $4 million to the new major events and tourism fund.

Division II creates chapter 15G. The economic development authority board may give grants to Iowa nonprofit economic development and tourism entities for bid, hosting, sanctioning and operating costs of athletic contests, conventions and music or art festivals. Recipients must put up a 50% match, administration is capped at 5% of the fund, and funding decisions are exempt from chapter 17A.

Division III narrows chapter 15F to an infrastructure-only program and repeals the sports tourism marketing fund (15F.403), transferring its remaining balance to the 15G fund (Sec. 23). Entities cannot receive assistance under both programs.
IA-SF660.comparison: No other states' bills were listed for comparison. What stands out is that the title says the bill relates to sports wagering, yet it contains nothing on operators, tax rates, licensing or wagering conduct. Its only link to wagering is using the 8.57I receipts fund as a funding source. The notable step is turning a fund previously spent 'as directed by the general assembly' into a source of permanent and formula-driven claims: the $8 million yearly public safety appropriation and the uncapped length of service award top-up.
IA-SF660.watch: The new standing claims on the sports wagering receipts fund (the $8 million yearly public safety appropriation and the open-ended length of service award top-up) make the state more dependent on sports wagering revenue, which could add pressure in future sessions to raise the wagering tax or fees if receipts fall short.

LA-HB639.summary: Act 298 raises Louisiana's tax on net gaming proceeds from online sports wagering (website or mobile app) from 15% to 21.5% under R.S. 27:625(B), leaving retail wagering through a sports wagering mechanism untouched. It redirects 25% of online sports wagering tax collections to a new Supporting Programs, Opportunities, Resources, and Teams (SPORTS) Fund for Division I university athletic departments and 3% to the Louisiana Postsecondary Inclusive Education Fund, with the remainder going to the state general fund. Despite the digest title, the enrolled text contains no video poker provisions.
mechanics: R.S. 27:625(B): online sports wagering tax rises from 15% to 21.5% of net gaming proceeds; electronic wagering through an in-person sports wagering mechanism is expressly excluded.
R.S. 27:625(G)(8): 25% of Subsection B collections go to the new SPORTS Fund (R.S. 17:1792), after Subsection D obligations are met.
R.S. 27:625(G)(9)-(10): 3% goes to the Louisiana Postsecondary Inclusive Education Fund (R.S. 17:3138.11), and any remainder goes to the state general fund.

R.S. 17:1792: Board of Regents distributes SPORTS Fund money equally among public universities in FBS and FCS conferences. Permitted uses are scholarships, insurance, medical coverage, facility enhancements, litigation settlement fees and Alston awards, and the money may not supplant other awards.
The text states no separate effective date or change to deductions, licensing or enforcement. The fiscal note estimates about +$34.7 million in revenue.
LA-HB639.comparison: Colorado HB 25-1311 raises effective tax by restricting operators' deductions against the existing 10% rate, whereas Louisiana HB 639 simply raises the headline online rate by 6.5 points and leaves the deduction base alone. Iowa SF 613 and SSB 1157 combine tax rate and license fee changes with gambling enforcement and dedicate revenue to tourism and major events; Louisiana instead earmarks a fixed share to college athletics, including Alston awards and litigation settlement costs. Hawaii HB 1308 and HB 2570 and Georgia HB 686 would legalize and tax sports betting from scratch, while Iowa SF 605 deals only with winnings withholding.
LA-HB639.watch: Operators should watch the split between online and retail rates and the definition of "sports wagering mechanism" in 27:625(B), and should expect the college-athletics earmark to create a constituency for further online rate increases.

CO-SB131.summary: SB 26-131 layers consumer-protection limits onto Colorado's existing sports betting regime. It bans solicitation push notifications, caps deposits at six per gaming day, prohibits credit card funding, and restricts advertising aimed at under-21 audiences. It also requires annual transactional data submissions, tightens integrity reporting to sports governing bodies, and lets leagues petition to restrict any type of wager on their events.
mechanics: Online operators may not send push notifications, including texts shown when the app is not open, that solicit bets or deposits (44-30-1501(8.7), 44-30-1506(8)(b)). Deposits are capped at six per individual per operator-defined 24-hour gaming day (1506(8)(a)(II)).

Accepting credit card deposits, directly or indirectly (including via accounts funded by a credit card), is unlawful under 44-30-1511(1)(d). Violations carry a monetary penalty of up to $25,000, in addition to or instead of suspension or revocation (44-30-524(1)(b)(III)).

New 44-30-1506.5 bars operators and their marketing affiliates (paid promoters, excluding broadcasters) from targeting under-21s or creating content clearly meant for them. It also bars advertising on any media whose audience is reasonably expected to be majority under-21, with an exception for public venues where attendee demographics cannot be determined.

Integrity reports under 1506(5)(a)(II)-(III) must now be made 'as soon as practicable' and sent simultaneously to the relevant sports governing body. The division and operators must use 'reasonable efforts' to cooperate with league investigations, replacing the earlier 'good and sufficient reason' standard. Leagues may petition the commission to restrict, limit, or exclude any type of wager on their events, no longer only single-player-outcome bets (1505(7)).

Starting February 1, 2028, and every February 1 after, online operators must submit all transactional data and metrics for the prior year, redacted of PII and exempt from CORA. The division publishes a compiled report by January 1, 2029 and every three years after (44-30-1507.5).

The act takes effect August 12, 2026 (assuming May 13 adjournment), unless a referendum petition is filed, and applies to conduct and agreements on or after that date. It also appropriates $124,623 and 0.5 FTE to the Department of Law, and requires the sports betting fund's water plan transfer to be no less than the prior year's (1509(2)(e)).
CO-SB131.comparison: Unlike the authorization bills listed (GA HB 686, HI HB 2570 and HB 1308), which create licensing and tax frameworks for new markets, Colorado's SB 131 imposes operational restrictions on a mature legal market. It also differs from tax-focused measures such as LA HB 639 and enforcement-against-illegal-operators bills such as AR HB 1861, because it targets licensed operators' marketing, payment, and engagement practices. Its combination of a hard deposit-frequency cap, a solicitation push-notification ban, and a credit card prohibition with a specific $25,000 penalty is unusual among the listed bills, as is mandatory annual data disclosure feeding a public triennial report.
CO-SB131.watch: Operators should watch how the commission interprets several open provisions: the scope of 'relating to the solicitation of bets or deposits' for push notifications, 'indirectly' funded credit card deposits (such as e-wallets or PayPal backed by cards), affiliate liability under the majority-under-21 audience test, and the breadth of 'all transactional data and metrics,' since these will drive compliance costs from August 12, 2026 onward.

IA-SSB1157.summary: SSB 1157 (renumbered SF 613) raises Iowa's sports wagering tax on net receipts from 6.75% to 9%. It replaces the graduated casino adjusted gross receipts tax with flat rates and doubles the casino annual license fee. It also shifts DCI gaming enforcement funding from licensee regulatory fees to an off-the-top credit of AGR tax, and redirects sports wagering receipts to public safety equipment ($8M a year) and a new $15M Iowa Major Events and Tourism Fund.
mechanics: Sports wagering tax under Iowa Code 99F.11(5)(a) rises from 6.75% to 9% of sports wagering net receipts (Sec. 15); Division I takes effect January 1, 2026 (Sec. 16).

The casino AGR tax drops the 5% (first $1M) and 10% (next $2M) tiers and the variable racetrack rates; it becomes a flat 22% for excursion boats and gambling structures and 24.125% for racetrack enclosures, whether or not they hold a table games license (Secs. 11-12).
The annual license fee for excursion gambling boats and gambling structures doubles from $5 to $10 per person of capacity (Sec. 6).

The DCI enforcement-cost component of the 99D.14 and 99F.10 regulatory fees is struck (Secs. 3-10). From FY2026-27, AGR tax is instead credited to the gaming enforcement revolving fund up to the amount appropriated to DPS, before the remainder goes to the rebuild Iowa infrastructure fund (Sec. 14). Internet fantasy sports background-check fees under 99E.4(4) are unchanged.

Beginning FY2026-27, $8M a year is appropriated from the sports wagering receipts fund to the public safety equipment fund (Sec. 1). A one-time $15M for FY2025-26 goes to the new Iowa Major Events and Tourism Fund under new chapter 15G (Sec. 21).

The new 15G program gives grants to Iowa nonprofits for bid, hosting and sanctioning costs of major events, with a 50% match requirement and a 5% administrative cap (Secs. 17-20). The sports tourism marketing fund (15F.403) is repealed and its balance transferred to the new fund (Secs. 31-32).
IA-SSB1157.comparison: Like LA HB 639, which raises Louisiana's online sports wagering tax and dedicates gaming revenue, SSB 1157 combines a sports betting rate increase with earmarks of the proceeds. Its 9% rate on net receipts remains low by national standards. CO HB 25-1311 takes a different route to more revenue: it keeps Colorado's 10% rate but narrows the deductions operators can take in calculating net proceeds, whereas Iowa raises the headline rate and leaves the net receipts base untouched. Unlike GA HB 686 and HI HB 1308/HB 2570, which would legalize and build sports wagering regimes from scratch, Iowa's bill adjusts an existing market and pairs the sports tax change with a flattening of land-based casino AGR taxes that eliminates the low-revenue tiers.
IA-SSB1157.watch: Operators should watch whether the 9% rate survives in SF 613 or is raised further, and how a January 1, 2026 effective date applies to a tax imposed on receipts 'each fiscal year', which could mean mid-year proration or partial-year compliance issues. Casino-affiliated licensees should also watch the loss of the 5%/10% AGR tiers and the doubled per-capacity license fee.

CA-AB1840.summary: AB 1840 adds Government Code Section 87451 to bar public officials, designated employees, and lobbyists from knowingly trading prediction market contracts on elections, administrative actions, legislative actions, or governmental decisions in their official duties while holding, or reasonably expecting to obtain through those duties, material nonpublic information about the transaction. It also amends Section 86205 so that a violation of 87451 is a prohibited lobbyist act. Violations carry Political Reform Act penalties, including misdemeanor liability.
mechanics: Covered persons (Sec. 87451(b)(1)): elected or appointed state or local public officials, Section 87200 filers, designated employees under Section 82019, and lobbyists under Section 82039.

Covered transactions (Sec. 87451(b)(2)): purchase, sale, or exchange of a prediction market contract on administrative actions or elections (both as defined in Sec. 82002), on governmental decisions made in the covered person's official duties, or on actions before the Legislature (Sec. 87102.5(b)(1)).

Prediction market contract (Sec. 87451(b)(4)): any contract, derivative, financial instrument, or investment issued, listed, or offered by a business entity that relates to the outcome, occurrence, or nonoccurrence of a future event; the definition is not limited to CFTC-registered platforms.

Knowledge standard: the person must knowingly trade while possessing material nonpublic information, or while it is reasonably foreseeable they may obtain it in their official duties. MNPI uses a 'reasonable investor' significance test.

Enforcement: misdemeanor under the Political Reform Act. The bill amends an initiative statute, so it needs a 2/3 vote of each house. It is fiscal and contains a state-mandated local program with no reimbursement (Sec. 3).
Status: introduced February 11, 2026; the second committee hearing was canceled at the author's request on April 9, 2026.
CA-AB1840.comparison: AB 1840 is closest to NY S09825, which also restricts public officers and legislative staff from trading on information gained in official duties. The New York bill also reaches mobile sports wagering platforms, while AB 1840 covers only prediction market contracts on political and governmental events and also reaches lobbyists and local officials. Unlike the platform-facing regimes in IL HB5059 and NY S09414 (ORACLE Acts), MN HF 4437/SF 4511, NC H1171, and VT H0913, it imposes no obligations or bans on operators and does not treat prediction markets as gambling (contrast IL HB5142). It also contains no tax (contrast NJ A5336/S4447) and no age limits (contrast CT HB05038).
CA-AB1840.watch: Operators listing election or policy event contracts should watch whether amendments add platform-side duties such as KYC screening of covered persons, reporting, or account restrictions, and should note that the broad 'prediction market contract' definition could later be borrowed for operator-facing regulation; the canceled hearing suggests the bill may be stalled this session.

AK-HB145.summary: HB 145 creates a new AS 05.18 authorizing mobile-only sports wagering in Alaska, administered by the Commissioner of Revenue, with up to 10 licenses at $100,000 per year and a 20 percent tax on adjusted gross revenue. Applicants must already hold a mobile sports wagering license (directly or through an affiliate or partner) in at least three other states. The bill also excludes AS 05.18 activity from the criminal definition of gambling and authorizes interstate wagering agreements.
mechanics: Licensing (AS 05.18.010): cap of 10 licenses. The license fee is $100,000 for the initial license and for each annual renewal, plus an optional processing fee. Licenses are non-transferable and require licensure in at least three other states. If applicants exceed slots, the commissioner awards licenses on past experience, projected AGR and projected tax revenue. Applicants must disclose holders of 15 percent or more and submit fingerprint-based or recent out-of-state criminal history checks.

Tax (AS 05.18.090): 20 percent of adjusted gross revenue, defined as wagers less winnings, voided bets and federal excise taxes. Promotional credits are not deductible. Returns and electronic payment are due by the 15th of each month. Negative AGR may be carried forward for up to three years with no carryback or refund unless the license is surrendered. Licensees are exempt from municipal wagering taxes.

Permitted wagers (AS 05.18.060 and .070): single-game bets, parlays, teasers, props, in-play bets, futures, pools and exchange wagering. Wagering events include collegiate and esports events but exclude events where most participants are under 18, other than the Olympics. Bettors must be 21 or older and located in Alaska or in a jurisdiction with an interstate agreement. Layoff wagers between licensees are allowed.

Operator duties (AS 05.18.030 and .050): integrity monitoring software and reporting of suspicious activity, including under 31 C.F.R. 1021.320 SAR rules. Operators must verify identity, advertise to no one under 21, obtain approval of house rules, and display 1-800-GAMBLER. Accounts may be funded by credit card, bonuses and promotions, ACH or e-wallets.

Enforcement (AS 05.18.110): penalties of up to $10,000 per violation, plus suspension or revocation and power to require termination of employees. Section 1 also requires ABC Board liquor license suspension for repeat AS 05.18 violations. Fantasy contests are excluded from the definition.
Effective dates: January 1, 2026, with the regulations section effective immediately. Operations cannot begin until at least three licenses are issued, and the public must receive 14 days' notice.
AK-HB145.comparison: Like GA HB 686 and the Hawaii bills (HB 1308, HB 2570, SB1569), HB 145 would legalize sports wagering from scratch, but it is mobile-only and housed in the Department of Revenue rather than a gaming commission. The Hawaii bills use a general excise tax on operator licenses, whereas Alaska uses a flat 20 percent AGR tax. HB 145's $100,000 annual fee is far below the $15 million license fee proposed in IL HB2878 and HB5034. Its explicit municipal tax exemption parallels IL HB4171's preemption of local sports wagering taxes. Unlike CT HB05229, it contains only a minimal under-21 advertising restriction and no AI or withdrawal rules.
AK-HB145.watch: Operators should watch whether the 20 percent rate, the lack of a promotional-credit deduction, the three-state licensure prerequisite and the 10-license cap with discretionary selection survive committee review in Labor and Commerce and in Finance. They should also watch whether the commissioner's regulations, which may apply retroactively under Section 6(b), add burdens beyond the statute.
