AK-SB194.summary: SB 194 legalizes statewide mobile-only sports wagering in Alaska under a new AS 05.18, administered by the Department of Revenue. It allows up to 10 one-year licenses at $100,000 each and taxes adjusted gross revenue at 20 percent. It also carves licensed wagering out of the criminal gambling definition in AS 11.66.280(3) and adds fingerprint-based background checks for licensees.
mechanics: Licensing (AS 05.18.010): applicants must hold, or have a subsidiary, partner or joint operating agreement with someone holding, a mobile sports wagering license in at least three other states, and must show their platform has been certified by an independent lab in another US jurisdiction. The fee is $100,000 per year plus a discretionary processing fee. Licenses are non-transferable and capped at 10; if oversubscribed, the commissioner picks based on experience, projected AGR and projected tax revenue.

Tax (AS 05.18.090): 20 percent of adjusted gross revenue, defined as handle less winnings, voided bets and federal excise tax, with no deduction for promotional credits. Returns and payment are due electronically by the 15th of each month. Negative AGR may be carried forward for up to three years, with no carryback or refund unless the licensee surrenders its license. Licensees are exempt from municipal wagering taxes.

Permitted wagers (AS 05.18.060 and .190): explicitly includes proposition, in-play, parlays, teasers, pools, exchange wagering and futures. Wagering events cover collegiate, amateur, professional, esports and motor racing, but exclude events where most participants are under 18 (Olympics excepted). Fantasy contests are excluded from the definition.

Player and conduct rules: bettors must be 21 or older and physically in Alaska or in a jurisdiction with an interstate agreement. Licensees may not advertise to under-21s, must display 1-800-GAMBLER, must get house rules approved, must report suspicious activity including SAR-type disclosures under 31 C.F.R. 1021.320, and may accept funding by card, bank transfer, online payment systems and bonuses.
Enforcement: civil penalties of up to $10,000 per violation, plus suspension, revocation, restriction, cease-and-desist and closure orders. Application information stays confidential for 25 years.

Timing: the Act takes effect January 1, 2026, with the regulations section effective immediately. Operations cannot start until at least three licenses are issued and the Department gives 14 days' public notice.
AK-SB194.comparison: Like GA HB 686 and the Hawaii bills (HB 1308, HB 2570, SB1569), SB 194 is a ground-up legalization bill. Unlike the Hawaii bills, which place regulation in the Department of Law Enforcement or DBEDT and use a general excise tax on operator licenses, Alaska gives the Department of Revenue sole regulatory authority and imposes a flat 20 percent AGR tax. Its $100,000 annual fee is modest compared with the $15 million master license fee proposed in IL HB2878 and HB5034. Its express exemption from municipal wagering taxes mirrors the home-rule preemption in IL HB4171.
AK-SB194.watch: Watch the three-other-states licensure prerequisite and the 10-license cap with selection based partly on projected tax revenue, both of which favour incumbent national operators, as well as the AGR definition that does not allow a deduction for promotional play at the 20 percent rate.

CT-HB5038.summary: Governor's Bill 5038 imposes consumer-protection conduct rules on prediction market platforms serving Connecticut residents: a 21+ age floor with age and geolocation verification, mandatory voluntary self-exclusion and spend-limit tools, and advertising restrictions aimed at under-21 audiences and college campuses, enforced by Attorney General civil penalties. It does not license, tax or ban prediction markets. It expressly carves out sports wagering, online casino gaming and internet games regulated under chapter 229b, and includes a federal-preemption savings clause. A separate section directs DCP, consulting the AG and the Mohegan and Mashantucket Pequot tribes, to study prediction markets' effects, including on master wagering licensee revenue, and report by February 1, 2027.
mechanics: Definitions (Sec. 1(a)): a 'prediction market' is any system letting state residents open speculative positions on future-event outcomes in a bid-ask format, regardless of mechanism. It excludes chapter 229b sports wagering, online casino gaming and internet games, and bid-asks tracking security, commodity or interest-rate prices or broad economic measures.

Age and access (Sec. 1(b)-(d)): no registration or positions for anyone under 21. Platforms must verify age 21+ and physical presence in the state before an account opens, and must offer self-exclusion from account creation or trading plus spend limits. On discovering an underage user, the platform must suspend the account, close all positions, pay out funds and bar the user until age 21.

Advertising (Sec. 2): every ad must state the 21+ requirement, and direct or targeted messages need a one-click unsubscribe link. Barred: ads aimed exclusively or primarily at under-21s or college campuses, targeting of self-excluded consumers, imagery or celebrity endorsements appealing to under-21s, misleading content, and placement in media or audiences that are majority or presumed majority under 21.
Enforcement (Sec. 3): AG civil penalty up to $10,000 per violation, rising to $50,000 per violation for a persistent course of conduct. DCP is to adopt implementing regulations (Sec. 4).

Effective dates: Secs. 1-5 take effect July 1, 2027. The Sec. 6 study takes effect July 1, 2026, with its report due February 1, 2027. Sec. 5 provides that any provision a court finds preempted by conflicting federal law yields to federal law.
CT-HB5038.comparison: CT HB05038 closely tracks the age-21, registration and verification framework in IL HB5059 and NY S09414 (both ORACLE Acts), but strips it down to a minors-and-advertising regime with AG penalties and no licensing. It contrasts with MN HF 4437/SF 4511 and NC H1171, which would prohibit prediction market wagering outright, and with IL HB5142, which would fold sports-event prediction markets into the Sports Wagering Act; Connecticut instead expressly excludes chapter 229b sports wagering from its definition. Unlike NJ A5336/S4447, it imposes no tax, and its advertising restrictions resemble NY S 10092's minors-focused approach. Distinctively, the Sec. 6 study must measure prediction markets' impact on tribal master wagering licensee revenue and state payments.
CT-HB5038.watch: Operators should watch whether the Sec. 6 study (consulting the Mohegan and Mashantucket Pequot tribes, report due February 1, 2027) becomes the basis for later legislation treating sports-event contracts as unlicensed sports wagering, and whether DCP regulations or preemption litigation over CFTC-regulated event contracts reshape the bill's light-touch, non-licensing approach before its July 1, 2027 effective date.

CT-HB5229.summary: Public Act 26-53 tightens Connecticut's consumer-protection and advertising rules for online gaming and sports wagering licensees. It newly bars gaming advertising in college athletic facilities and on college-run digital channels, and requires geolocation controls for fantasy-only and online lottery/keno platforms. It also orders a Department of Consumer Protection study of prediction markets (report due February 1, 2027) and revises lottery game testing and certification procedures.
mechanics: Sec. 1 (eff. July 1, 2026) amends CGS 12-863(c). Master wagering licensees, online gaming operators, service providers and sports wagering retailers must set up a toll-free number for help resolving platform problems; a prerecorded message routing users to online help is allowed. The number must be displayed conspicuously on each website and app, alongside the existing problem-gambling line, self-exclusion link, time-on-site display, break-in-play tool and balance display.

Sec. 2 (eff. July 1, 2026) amends 12-863(e). A new subdivision (9) bars gaming advertising in athletic facilities on any public or private college campus in Connecticut, and on any website, social media, online service or app run by or for such an institution. The only exception is an announcement, signage or display directed to a general audience.

Sec. 2 also bars ads pertaining exclusively to keno, online lottery or fantasy contests from TV programs aimed primarily at under-18s, judged by a nationally recognized content rating system, and from ad breaks during those programs. The existing ban on targeting self-excluded individuals now expressly covers Internet games and retail sports wagering.

Sec. 3 (eff. from passage) directs the DCP Commissioner to study prediction market platforms, consulting the Attorney General, the Mohegan Tribe, the Mashantucket Pequot Tribe and the Connecticut Lottery Corporation. Topics include under-21 use and advertising, problem gambling, the most common positions taken, and effects on master wagering licensee revenue and state payments. The report is due February 1, 2027.

Sec. 4 (eff. from passage) covers platforms offering exclusively fantasy contests or online lottery draw/keno sales. Their geolocation systems must defeat or block proxies and VPNs, check location at each entry fee or purchase, block transactions when location cannot be determined and show a pop-up, and flag geographically inconsistent account access.

Sec. 5 amends CGS 12-806a(c). Lottery draw games sold in at least 20 states and tested by a lab licensed in at least 20 states are exempt from Connecticut lab certification. DCP may publish technical standards, with updates effective 30 days after posting. Revocation authority and the 'without notice' language are removed; suspension is now allowed where continued operation 'could reasonably cause substantial detriment to the public interest.'
CT-HB5229.comparison: Unlike IL HB5059 (ORACLE Act), which would directly bar under-21s from prediction markets and impose platform duties, Connecticut stops at a study. That study expressly measures prediction markets' effect on master wagering licensee revenue and state payments, which signals possible protective legislation in 2027. Bills such as AK HB145/SB194, GA HB 686 and HI HB 1308/SB1569 would create new sports wagering markets. HB05229 instead fine-tunes an existing regime's responsible-gaming, marketing and geolocation rules. Its campus-advertising ban is a targeted conduct rule rather than the broad market overhaul in FL H0189.
CT-HB5229.watch: Operators should audit college sponsorships, in-venue signage and university digital placements against the new Sec. 2(9) campus advertising ban, and have the new customer-assistance toll-free number live and displayed by July 1, 2026. They should also track the February 2027 prediction-market report, since its revenue-impact findings could drive competitive or restrictive legislation.

DC-B26-0340.summary: This is D.C.'s omnibus FY2026 Budget Support emergency act, and nearly all of it deals with non-gaming budget matters. Two subtitles in Title II are gaming-relevant. Subtitle G (Secs. 2061-2064) carves bingo, sports wagering and games of skill out of the D.C. gaming-contract statute (D.C. Code § 16-1702) and reworks game-of-skill machine licensing between the Office of Lottery and Gaming (OLG) and the Alcoholic Beverage and Cannabis Administration (ABCA); Subtitle H (Secs. 2071-2073) creates a new 'commercial bingo' category limited to on-premises alcohol licensees.
mechanics: Sec. 2062 adds § 16-1702(b)-(d) so that subsection (a) does not apply to: commercial bingo under § 36-601.01 et seq.; sports wagering under § 36-621.01 et seq. as of May 3, 2019; and games of skill under § 36-641.01 et seq. as of April 27, 2021. This is a retroactive carve-out from the gaming-contract statute.

Games of skill (Secs. 2063-2064): a game of skill retailer must hold a retailer's license plus a game of skill machine endorsement under § 25-113.01(e). ABCA, not OLG, processes and issues retailer's licenses (new § 36-641.08(a-1)). OLG must promptly notify ABCA of any citation, revocation or other enforcement action (new § 36-641.16(f)). A § 25-508 fee is raised from $200 to $500/year.

Commercial bingo is defined as bingo played for consideration, with numbers drawn and called aloud by a person physically present with the players (new § 36-601.01(c)(4A)). Bingo is defined as a 75-ball game on 5x5 cards. The definition excludes charitable bingo under § 36-601.23(b)-(d), bingo played on federal gambling devices (15 U.S.C. 1171(a)), and online or class II facsimile play.

Only on-premises alcohol licensees in the listed classes (C/R, D/R, C/T, D/T, C/H, D/H, C/X, D/X, C/RB, D/RB, C/N, D/N) may offer commercial bingo. They need both an ABC Board endorsement ($300/year) and an OLG license, and OLG may not issue any commercial bingo license before October 1, 2025.

Sec. 2073(b) renames § 36-601.12 the 'Lottery, Gambling, and Gaming Fund' and excludes from it funds generated by the tax under §§ 47-2002(a)(9) and 47-2202(a)(6). The rate of that tax is not shown in the supplied text.

The CFO must adopt rules on the conduct of bingo and raffles to ensure integrity and fair play (rewritten § 36-601.24). The supplied text is truncated at this point, so the remaining rule requirements are not visible.
DC-B26-0340.comparison: No comparable bills from other states are listed. What stands out is that a budget support act retroactively exempts legal sports wagering (back to May 3, 2019) and games of skill (back to April 27, 2021) from D.C.'s gaming-contract statute. Effectively, this is a legislative fix that shores up the enforceability of wagering transactions. The act also creates a narrowly fenced commercial bingo product: in person, live-called, alcohol-licensee only, and expressly excluding online or electronic play.
DC-B26-0340.watch: Operators should confirm how the retroactive § 16-1702(c) carve-out for sports wagering affects litigation risk over pre-enactment wagers, and should watch whether the truncated bingo provisions or the separate §§ 47-2002(a)(9)/47-2202(a)(6) tax are later extended toward electronic or online formats.

DC-B26-0450.summary: This is the District's omnibus FY2026 budget support emergency act. Most of it is unrelated to gaming, but two subtitles matter. Subtitle G retroactively exempts licensed sports wagering (as of May 3, 2019) and games of skill (as of April 27, 2021) from D.C. Code § 16-1702(a), and tightens alcohol-license integration for game-of-skill machines. Subtitle H creates a new commercial bingo regime limited to on-premises alcohol licensees, who need both an ABCA endorsement and an Office of Lottery and Gaming (OLG) license.
mechanics: Sec. 2062 designates the existing text of D.C. Code § 16-1702 as subsection (a) and adds carve-outs: (a) does not apply to commercial bingo, does not apply to sports wagering under § 36-621.01 et seq. as of May 3, 2019, and does not apply to games of skill under § 36-641.01 et seq. as of April 27, 2021.

Game of skill (Secs. 2063-2064): the § 25-508 fee rises from $200 to $500/year, and § 25-113.01(e)(1) drops the 'on-site sales and consumption permit' holder category. A retailer must hold a retailer's license plus a game of skill machine endorsement, ABCA takes over processing and issuing retailer's licenses, and OLG must notify ABCA of citations, revocations or other enforcement against a licensed establishment.

Commercial bingo definition (Sec. 2073, new § 36-601.01(c)(4A)): bingo played for consideration, with a 75-ball draw announced by a caller physically present with the players. It excludes charitable bingo under § 36-601.23(b)-(d), bingo on gambling devices as defined in 15 U.S.C. 1171(a), and online bingo or Class II facsimile machines as defined in 25 U.S.C. 2703(7).

Commercial bingo licensing: only on-premises retailers in classes C/R, D/R, C/T, D/T, C/H, D/H, C/X, D/X, C/RB, D/RB, C/N and D/N may offer it. Each needs an ABC Board commercial bingo endorsement ($300/year) plus an OLG license, and OLG may not issue licenses before October 1, 2025. The CFO must adopt integrity rules for bingo and raffles.

Funds: the lottery fund at § 36-601.12 is renamed the 'Lottery, Gambling, and Gaming Fund', and revenue from the taxes imposed by §§ 47-2002(a)(9) and 47-2202(a)(6) is excluded from it. The supplied text is truncated, so the substance of those tax provisions is not visible.

Duration: this is a congressional-review emergency act, published at 72 DCR 890, that expires February 22, 2026. Durable effect depends on the companion permanent FY2026 Budget Support Act (D.C. Act 26-148).
DC-B26-0450.comparison: No other states' bills were listed for comparison. The unusual feature is that a budget support vehicle carries a retroactive statutory carve-out shielding licensed sports wagering, dating back to the May 3, 2019 effective date of DC's sports wagering law, from the general gaming provision in § 16-1702. It does so alongside a narrowly drawn, in-person-only commercial bingo authorization that expressly bars electronic, online and Class II-style formats.
DC-B26-0450.watch: Confirm that the retroactive § 16-1702 sports-wagering carve-out, which is significant for defending loss-recovery or contract-voidness claims against licensed operators, is carried into permanent law before this emergency act lapses on February 22, 2026, and review the truncated commercial bingo tax provisions (§§ 47-2002(a)(9), 47-2202(a)(6)) for any spillover onto other gaming revenue.

DC-B26-0265.summary: The District's omnibus FY2026 budget support act, effective December 6, 2025, includes two gaming subtitles among dozens of unrelated provisions. Subtitle G (Sec. 2062) retroactively exempts sports wagering (as of May 3, 2019) and games of skill (as of April 27, 2021) from D.C. Code § 16-1702(a), and moves game-of-skill retailer licensing to ABCA. Subtitle H creates a regulated commercial bingo category limited to on-premises alcohol licensees, who must hold both an ABC Board endorsement and an Office of Lottery and Gaming license.
mechanics: Sec. 2062 adds § 16-1702(b)-(d): subsection (a) does not apply to commercial bingo under § 36-601.01 et seq., to sports wagering under Subchapter II of Chapter 6 of Title 36 as of May 3, 2019, or to games of skill under Subchapter III as of April 27, 2021.

Game of skill (Secs. 2063-2064): a retailer needs a retailer's license plus a game of skill machine endorsement under § 25-113.01(e). The fee in § 25-508 rises from $200 to $500/year. ABCA, not OLG, processes and issues retailer's licenses, and OLG must promptly notify ABCA of any citation, revocation or other enforcement against a licensed establishment.

Commercial bingo is defined (§ 36-601.01(c)(4A)) as bingo for consideration with numbers drawn and called by a person physically present with the players. It excludes charitable bingo, bingo on federally defined gambling devices, and online play or machines that would be a facsimile of IGRA class II gaming.

Only on-premises retailers in classes C/R, D/R, C/T, D/T, C/H, D/H, C/X, D/X, C/RB, D/RB, C/N and D/N may offer commercial bingo. They need a $300/year commercial bingo endorsement from the ABC Board and an OLG license, and no OLG license may issue before October 1, 2025.

The Lottery fund is renamed the 'Lottery, Gambling, and Gaming Fund'. Revenue from the taxes at §§ 47-2002(a)(9) and 47-2202(a)(6) is carved out of the deposit rule, though the visible text does not show what those taxes are.

The CFO must adopt rules on bingo and raffle integrity and fair play, covering application requirements, fees, and device and technology configurations. The enrolled text supplied is truncated mid-section, so the remaining rulemaking items and any later gaming provisions are not visible.
DC-B26-0265.comparison: No other states' bills were listed for comparison. On its own, the act is unusual because it uses a budget vehicle to declare, retroactive to the 2019 launch of DC sports wagering, that § 16-1702(a) does not apply to authorized sports wagering. It also creates a narrowly drawn, in-person-only commercial bingo category that expressly bars electronic, online and class II-style formats, and it splits gaming licensing between ABCA and OLG.
DC-B26-0265.watch: Confirm the scope and retroactive effect of the new § 16-1702(c) carve-out for sports wagering, which appears aimed at foreclosing challenges under the District's general gaming statute to bets placed since May 3, 2019. Also track the CFO bingo rules, the as-yet-unseen tax provisions at §§ 47-2002(a)(9) and 47-2202(a)(6), and any expansion of the ABCA licensing role that could reach sports-wagering retail partners.

DE-HB314.summary: HB314 creates a new crime of student athlete harassment (new 28 Del. C. § 908) covering threats and sports-related bullying or cyber-bullying of intercollegiate student athletes tied to their athletic performance, and gives convicted offenders' victims a private right of action with $75,000 minimum statutory damages per violation. It also amends the lottery exclusion statute (29 Del. C. § 4835) so that people convicted under § 908 are mandatorily placed on the exclusion list for video lottery, table, Internet lottery and sports lottery games. It further lets the Lottery Director emergency-exclude from sports lottery play anyone charged with, or found to have threatened, such harassment, and directs the Director and the Division of Gaming Enforcement to set up a reporting channel for athletes and coaches.
mechanics: New § 908(b) offense: intentionally communicating a threat to a student athlete related to performance in an intercollegiate sport, judged on both a subjective intent and a reasonable-person test, or engaging in sports-related bullying or cyber-bullying, which must be repeated, intended to harm, and cause emotional distress.

Penalties under § 908(c): a first offense is a class A misdemeanor and a second or subsequent offense is a class E felony, with exclusive Superior Court jurisdiction; 'student athlete' and 'intercollegiate sport' are defined by cross-reference to 24 Del. C. § 5402.

Private right of action under § 908(e) against a person convicted of the offense, with at least $75,000 in statutory damages per intentional violation plus actual damages, punitive damages, equitable relief, costs and attorney fees.

Electronic communications providers are exempt when acting in the normal course of business, but social network operators serving Delaware must disclose log files and communications on a warrant, a court order based on specific and articulable facts, or user consent; providers get immunity for compliance and may move to quash unduly burdensome orders.

Amended § 4835(c)(3) lets the Director issue an emergency order excluding a person from sports lottery play if the person has been charged under § 908 or a similar out-of-state statute, or has threatened a student athlete over performance in an intercollegiate sport that is the subject of a sports lottery game; new § 4835(j) mandates placing anyone convicted under § 908 or a similar statute on the exclusion list.
New § 4835(k) requires the Director and the Division of Gaming Enforcement to establish and publicize a method for student athletes and intercollegiate coaches to report violations or threats.
DE-HB314.comparison: Unlike MD HB518, which pairs college athlete protections with problem-gambling and voluntary exclusion regulations, Delaware's bill is built around a new criminal offense and a civil damages remedy, with gaming exclusion as the enforcement hook. It resembles NY A 7903 and S07482 in designating people convicted of crimes against athletes as barred bettors, but NY places the duty to block accounts on account wagering licensees, while Delaware runs it through the State Lottery Director's exclusion list, because Delaware sports betting operates as a state lottery. It does not touch prop-bet restrictions like LA SB354 or NC H828, and it has nothing in common with the NIL bills listed (GA HB383, HI HB 2384, TX HB126).
DE-HB314.watch: Watch how the mandatory § 4835(j) exclusion list, which also reaches convictions under 'similar' statutes in other states, and the emergency exclusions based only on charges or threats will be passed to and enforced by Delaware's sports lottery vendors and casino licensees, including duties to screen accounts and to respond to the new reporting channel; note also that the bill's last recorded action, a failed motion to release on 2026-03-18, suggests it is stalled.

GA-HB383.summary: HB383 creates a new Article 32A in Title 20 of the Georgia Code that lets high school student athletes, including eighth graders and home-study participants, receive name, image, or likeness (NIL) compensation, subject to Commissioner of Labor consent under the child-labor provisions of Code Section 39-2-18. Among other limits, it bars NIL deals that can reasonably be perceived as endorsing or promoting casinos and gambling, including sports betting, the lottery, and betting tied to video, online, or mobile games. It also bars pay-for-enrollment and school or booster NIL payments, makes contracts expire automatically after graduation or withdrawal, and stops athletic associations from penalizing NIL activity.
mechanics: Section 20-2-2105.3(e)(7) prohibits a student athlete from receiving NIL compensation for any conduct that can reasonably be perceived as endorsing or promoting casinos and gambling, including sports betting, the lottery, and betting in connection with video games, online games, and mobile devices. The same list covers alcohol, tobacco, vapor, cannabis, firearms, and any product restricted to people under 18.

Revised Section 39-2-18(b)(4) requires the Commissioner of Labor, before giving the written consent needed for a minor's NIL compensation, to determine that the minor's NIL will not be used for any purpose barred by 20-2-2105.3(e). This builds the gambling ban into the state labor consent process.

Section 20-2-2105.3(b)-(d) bars NIL tied to attending a particular school or college, and bars payments from schools, boosters, or their agents. It also bans use of school marks or references to a school or association in NIL activity, and bars endorsing an NIL payor or its third-party partners during games and competitions (tryouts, practices, and training sessions are exempt).
Under Section 20-2-2105.6, NIL contracts cannot survive past the earlier of 10 days after graduation or 30 days after enrollment ends, and any noncompliant contract terms are void.

Under Sections 20-2-2105.7 and 20-2-2105.8, athletic associations may not penalize athletes or schools for permitted NIL activity. Publicly funded schools may not take part in associations whose governing documents do not comply, and athletes may hire certified agents or attorneys, with agents required to comply with the federal SPARTA.
Under Section 4, the Act takes effect on the Governor's approval (or on becoming law without it) and applies to contracts entered into or renewed on or after that date.
GA-HB383.comparison: Unlike CT HB05229, which restricts gaming advertising on college campuses directly through gaming licensees, HB383 places the gambling restriction on the minor's ability to accept NIL compensation rather than on operators. It is also unlike MD HB518, which pairs problem-gambling regulations with college athlete protections inside the gaming code. Its closest analogues are LA HB 513 (interscholastic and intercollegiate NIL) and DE HB314 (student athlete protection), while HI HB 2384 and SB3263 address only university-level NIL. None of the listed summaries indicate that those bills contain an express sports-betting endorsement ban like Georgia's 20-2-2105.3(e)(7).
GA-HB383.watch: Operators should watch the broad 'reasonably can be perceived as endorsing or promoting' standard and the 'third-party partner' language, because sponsorships, affiliate marketing, or social-casino and sweepstakes-style promotions that touch high school athletes (including eighth graders) could be swept in even though the bill imposes no direct penalty on operators.

FL-H189.summary: CS/CS/CS/HB 189 is an omnibus Florida gambling-enforcement bill that tightens Florida Gaming Control Commission ethics and revolving-door rules, raises many gambling offenses from misdemeanors to felonies, and adds licensure consequences for gambling-house and slot-machine convictions. According to its title, it also expressly criminalizes Internet gambling and Internet sports wagering (amended s. 849.08), imposes requirements on fantasy sports contests (new s. 849.0932), prohibits certain gambling advertising (new s. 849.48), and preempts local ordinances (new s. 849.49). The House bill was laid on the table on 2026-03-11 in favor of CS/CS/SB 1580, so the Senate bill is now the live vehicle.
mechanics: Integrity: amended s. 838.12(3) makes it a third-degree felony to bet on any professional or amateur contest knowing the result is prearranged or fixed. Section 1 expands the Commission's annual report to cover complaints, seized property and forfeitures.

Revolving door: ss. 16.713 and 16.715 bar commissioners and employees from working for, owning, or contracting with any entity that 'conducts or facilitates an activity regulated, enforced, or investigated by the commission, including fantasy sports contests and other betting activities.' The bar runs for 2 years before service, during service, and for 2 years after.

Licensure: new s. 849.023 lets DBPR, the Commission (chs. 550, 551, s. 849.086) and OFR (ch. 560) summarily suspend or revoke a license after a conviction under s. 849.01, 849.03 or 849.15, regardless of adjudication. The same applies if a 'controlling person' (officer, director, or more than 5% equity holder) is convicted. The licensee faces a fine of up to $75,000 but can keep the license by removing the controlling person.

Criminal penalties: s. 849.01 (keeping a gambling house) moves from a second-degree misdemeanor to a third-degree felony. Sections 849.02 and 849.03 add escalating penalties, reaching a second-degree felony for repeat offenses. New s. 849.021 makes it a felony for a government employee to knowingly license, aid or conceal a gambling house.

Pari-mutuel ownership: s. 550.054(12) requires Commission pre-approval for ownership changes of 5% or more unless the owner was previously approved, and changes under 5% must be reported within 20 days. Escheated harness and thoroughbred permits can no longer be reissued.

Amusement machines: under s. 546.10(8), federally chartered veterans' organizations with liquor licenses may seek a binding declaratory statement on a machine, which the Commission must issue within 60 days. The option is unavailable if the machine or premises is under criminal investigation.
FL-H189.comparison: Unlike AK HB145/SB194, GA HB 686 and HI HB 1308/HB 2570/SB1569, which authorize, license and tax mobile sports wagering, FL H0189 goes the other way: it is a prohibition and enforcement bill that criminalizes Internet sports wagering outside existing exceptions. Its fantasy-contest provisions (s. 849.0932) sit in the criminal code with Attorney General and state attorney enforcement, unlike IL HB2342's Gaming Board licensing model for fantasy operators. Its advertising ban (s. 849.48) targets illegal gambling generally, rather than regulating licensed-operator marketing as CT HB05229 does.
FL-H189.watch: Track CS/CS/SB 1580, the live vehicle, for the final text of the s. 849.08 Internet sports wagering prohibition, the s. 849.0932 fantasy contest requirements and the s. 849.48 advertising ban, which are truncated in this excerpt; check how the exceptions are drawn, since offshore, DFS and pick'em operators and their vendors and advertisers could face felony exposure.

FL-S1580.summary: CS/CS/SB 1580 is a broad Florida illegal-gambling enforcement package. It sharply increases criminal penalties for keeping or facilitating gambling houses, creates new offenses (including betting on a fixed contest), and adds licensure consequences for businesses whose controlling persons commit gambling crimes. According to its title, it also criminalizes Internet gambling, Internet sports wagering and advertising of illegal gambling, preempts local gaming ordinances, and restructures Florida Gaming Control Commission governance and ethics rules; it died in returning messages on 2026-03-13.
mechanics: s. 849.01: keeping a gambling house, now expressly defined, moves from a second-degree misdemeanor to a third-degree felony for a first offense and a second-degree felony for repeat offenses (or where great bodily harm results). New s. 849.01(3) makes it a third-degree felony, with a mandatory $50,000 fine per violation, to knowingly or in reckless disregard benefit financially from, or participate in a 'course of conduct' providing any service, product or material benefit in furtherance of, a gambling house. Keeping a gambling house is also added as a felony-murder predicate in s. 782.04(3)(s).

s. 838.12(3) (new): staking, betting or wagering on any professional or amateur game, contest, match, race or sport with knowledge that the outcome is prearranged or predetermined is a third-degree felony.

s. 849.023 (new): violations of ss. 849.01, 849.03 or 849.15 are deemed an immediate and serious danger to public health, safety and welfare. DBPR, the Gaming Control Commission or OFR may summarily suspend licenses (alcohol, lodging, pari-mutuel, slot, cardroom, money services) of violators or of entities whose 'controlling person' commits them; a controlling person includes officers, directors and holders of more than 5% equity. Convictions, including withheld adjudication and nolo pleas, can lead to revocation, avoidable by removing the controlling person, and licensees face fines up to $75,000.

Per the bill title (operative text not reproduced in the excerpt provided), the bill also: amends s. 849.08 to define and criminalize playing, operating, conducting or promoting Internet gambling or Internet sports wagering; creates s. 849.48 criminalizing advertising of illegal gambling, with exceptions; creates s. 849.49 preempting local ordinances on certain gaming; and creates s. 849.155 on bulk slot-machine trafficking and a Limited Slot Machine Surrender Program offering immunity.

s. 849.021 (new): a government employee who knowingly certifies, licenses, approves, aids, facilitates or conceals a gambling house commits a third-degree felony, and a second-degree felony on a repeat offense.

Commission and industry changes: the full commission, rather than the chair, appoints the inspector general. Revolving-door restrictions for former staff are expanded to 2 years, covering employment with any regulated person or any party to a commission proceeding, subject to case-by-case waivers. Veterans' organizations may seek binding declaratory statements on amusement machines, decided within 60/90 days. Slot licensees may relocate gaming areas within 1,320 feet in the same county under s. 551.114(4)(b).
FL-S1580.comparison: Unlike the legalization-and-tax bills listed (AK HB145/SB194, GA HB 686, HI HB 1308/HB 2570/SB1569), FL S1580 does not authorize or tax any new wagering; it is a criminal enforcement bill aimed at unlicensed gambling, and, per its title, Internet sports wagering outside Florida's compact-based framework. CT HB05229 restricts advertising by licensed operators, whereas FL's advertising provision (per its title) targets promotion of illegal gambling. FL's match-fixing wagering offense in s. 838.12(3) is an integrity measure absent from the listed IL bills. Unlike IL HB5142 and HB5059, nothing in the reproduced FL text addresses prediction markets.
FL-S1580.watch: Although the bill died, a reintroduction would carry the s. 849.01(3) 'reckless disregard' facilitation offense, with a $50,000 per-violation fine, and the reported Internet sports wagering and advertising crimes, which could expose payment processors, suppliers, affiliates and media partners of any operator not authorized under Florida law; operators with Florida-licensed affiliates should also note that s. 849.023 lets regulators summarily suspend licenses based on the conduct of 5%-plus owners.

GA-HR753.summary: HR 753, as substituted by the House Rules Committee, is an omnibus study-committee resolution. Sections 1 and 2 create committees on rural internal medicine access and on paternity legitimation, and Section 3 creates the House Study Committee on Gaming in the State of Georgia. That committee is charged with studying the economic, fiscal, workforce and social impacts of legalizing destination resort casinos, pari-mutuel and fixed-odds horse racing, and digital, retail and on-premise sports betting, and with proposing legislation before it is abolished on December 1, 2025.
mechanics: Section 3(2): seven members, namely the chairs of the House Ways and Means, Regulated Industries, and Economic Development Committees plus four House members appointed by the Speaker, one of whom the Speaker designates as chair.
Section 3(4): the committee must hold at least four public hearings at various locations around the state and at least one meeting to finalize findings.

Section 3(6): unlike the other two committees, which may file a report, the gaming committee is directed that it 'shall adopt specific findings or recommendations that include proposed legislation' and must file a report before abolishment.

Scope per the whereas clauses: revenue and tax potential, job quality, social harms, gaming dollars lost to other states (Nevada, Mississippi, Alabama, North Carolina and Massachusetts are named), and horse-breeding industry benefits from pari-mutuel racing.
Funding comes from House appropriations, with member allowances under O.C.G.A. 28-1-8 capped at three days unless additional days are authorized; all committees are abolished December 1, 2025.
The resolution creates no legal authorization, tax rate or licensing regime. Any legalization would still require voter approval of a constitutional amendment and enabling legislation.
GA-HR753.comparison: No comparable bills from other states are listed. This is an unusual vehicle: a gaming study committee bundled into a resolution whose title concerns rural internal medicine. Unlike earlier Georgia legalization measures that went straight to constitutional amendments or enabling statutes, it sets up a pre-session fact-finding process that is required to produce draft legislation.
GA-HR753.watch: Operators should engage with the four or more statewide public hearings and the committee's mandatory proposed legislation due before December 1, 2025, since that report will likely shape the tax rate, mobile versus retail licensing structure, and any bundling of sports betting with casinos and horse racing in Georgia's 2026 session.

GA-HR450.summary: HR 450 is a proposed amendment to Article I, Section II, Paragraph VIII of the Georgia Constitution that would let the General Assembly authorize and regulate sports betting by general law, subject to voter ratification. It earmarks sports betting tax proceeds to a new Georgia Sports Betting Proceeds Trust Fund for problem-gambling programs and lottery-style education programs such as pre-K and HOPE scholarships. It also allows the Georgia Lottery Corporation to participate in sports betting. The resolution failed on House third reading on 2026-03-06.
mechanics: Rewritten subparagraph (a) keeps a constitutional ban, enforced by penal laws, on 'all forms of sports betting, pari-mutuel betting, and casino gambling' except as the Paragraph provides; only sports betting is carved out.

New subparagraph (d) authorizes the General Assembly to provide by law for operating and regulating sports betting. Tax proceeds go to the Georgia Sports Betting Proceeds Trust Fund. Other regulatory proceeds first cover regulatory operating expenses and reserves without appropriation, and the net remainder goes to the Trust Fund.

Subparagraph (e)(1) splits Trust Fund appropriations: 15% of the first $150 million each fiscal year goes to problem-gambling prevention and treatment, and 85% of the first $150 million plus everything above $150 million goes to voluntary pre-K and the existing lottery education purposes in subparagraph (c). Under (e)(2), the education share is exempt from the lapse rule in Art. III, Sec. IX, Para. IV(c).

Subparagraph (f) lets the Georgia Lottery Corporation be authorized by law to participate in sports betting. Its participation proceeds follow the lottery education rules in (c), while any tax imposed on its participation follows the Trust Fund rules in (e).
The amendment contains no tax rate, licensing structure, license cap, or mobile-versus-retail rules; all of that is left to implementing legislation.
Section 2 sets the ballot question: authorize sports betting 'to provide additional funding for pre-kindergarten and HOPE scholarships?' Ratification follows Art. X, Sec. I, Para. II.
GA-HR450.comparison: Alaska's HB145 and SB194 and Hawaii's HB 1308, HB 2570 and SB1569 are statutory frameworks that directly set licensing, regulators, and taxes for operators. HR 450 is only a constitutional enabling amendment with no operator-facing terms. Its distinctive features are that it hard-codes revenue earmarks into the constitution, including a problem-gambling carve-out capped at 15% of the first $150 million, and that it gives the state lottery corporation an express constitutional role. It also writes explicit prohibitions on pari-mutuel and casino gambling into the constitution. Illinois bills such as HB3159 and HB5143 instead adjust taxes within an already operating sports wagering regime.
GA-HR450.watch: The resolution lost on House third reading, so watch for reconsideration or a successor vehicle, and for whether companion enabling legislation uses subparagraph (f) to channel the market through the Georgia Lottery Corporation, which could shape whether private operators participate and on what terms.

HI-SB1569.summary: SB1569 SD1 would legalize mobile-only sports wagering in Hawaii under a new HRS chapter administered by the Department of Business, Economic Development, and Tourism (DBEDT), with at least four operator licenses restricted to "qualified gaming entities" already live in three or more U.S. states. It taxes adjusted gross sports wagering receipts at 10% through a new paragraph (9) of the general excise tax statute, section 237-13. It also carves sports wagering and fantasy sports contests out of the gambling definitions in section 712-1220. The SD1 carries a placeholder effective date of July 1, 2050 and blank criminal fine amounts and appropriation figures, signalling the bill is still a vehicle for negotiation.
mechanics: Licensing: DBEDT must issue a minimum of four operator licenses (section -5), open only to entities offering online sports wagering in at least three U.S. jurisdictions. The fee is $250,000 for a five-year term plus cost-based processing fees. A three-year temporary license is available on payment of the initial fee, and a universal start date must be set no later than 180 days after enactment.
Supplier licenses (section -6) cost $10,000 for five years, with temporary licenses available. Suppliers are oddly defined as providers of geolocation and age verification services.

Tax: 10% of adjusted gross sports wagering receipts under new HRS 237-13(9), on the accrual method, stated to be in lieu of all other taxes on sports wagering operations. Adjusted gross receipts are gross cash wagers less winnings paid. There is no promotional-credit deduction, and bonuses count as an account-funding method.

Product scope: mobile/digital only, with kiosks and retail terminals barred (section -10(c)). Bettors must be 21+ and physically in Hawaii. Collegiate, amateur, Olympic, motorsport and e-sports events are permitted, and wagering on events where most participants are under 18 is excluded. Exchange wagering, in-play and prop bets are expressly allowed, as are layoff bets between operators and interstate wagering agreements.

Operator duties (section -8): integrity monitoring software, with suspicious activity reported to DBEDT; 1-800-GAMBLER in all advertising; daily receipts records; DBEDT-approved house rules. There is also a voluntary self-exclusion program with lifetime option and at least quarterly list sharing, and an employee betting ban.

Enforcement: civil fines up to $5,000 per violation or $10,000 per occurrence, which can be imposed on unlicensed persons too. Unlicensed sports wagering escalates from a misdemeanor to a class C and then class B felony, with fine amounts left blank. A problem gambling special fund administered by the Department of Health is funded only by appropriation.
HI-SB1569.comparison: Like AK HB145 and SB194, SB1569 is a mobile-only legalization bill in a state with no existing casino industry, so licenses go to out-of-state online operators rather than being tethered to land-based venues. Its 10% GGR rate is low compared with the steep rate and license-fee proposals in Illinois, for example IL HB2878 and HB5034 setting a $15 million master license fee. Unlike CT HB05229 or IL HB5059, it contains no detailed advertising, AI-targeting or prediction-market provisions beyond the 1-800-GAMBLER requirement. Unlike GA HR450 and SR131, it proceeds by statute without a constitutional amendment.
HI-SB1569.watch: Watch whether the 2050 placeholder effective date, the blank fine amounts and the 10% rate are reset in the 2026 session. Also watch whether the 'minimum of four' license language and the three-jurisdiction qualification gate stay intact, along with the absence of a promotional-play deduction, since these will determine market access and effective tax burden.

GA-SR131.summary: SR131 is a proposed amendment to the Georgia Constitution (Art. I, Sec. II, Para. VIII) that would let the General Assembly authorize and regulate sports betting and casino gambling by statute, administered by a gaming commission it must create. The amendment fixes the tax rate and dedicates the proceeds to a new Georgia Gaming Proceeds Fund, with large set-asides for county governments and problem-gambling programs. It takes effect only if passed by the legislature and ratified by voters on the stated ballot question.
mechanics: New subpara. (e)(1)-(2): the General Assembly may provide by law for sports betting and casino gambling and must create a gaming commission with regulatory and taxing powers. Revised subpara. (a) expressly lists sports betting, pari-mutuel betting and casino gambling as prohibited except as provided, and nothing in (e) authorizes pari-mutuel betting.

Subpara. (e)(3) on casinos: at least eight casino gaming licenses, each for a single facility. No person or entity may hold more than one license or own an interest in more than one licensee. No off-site casino gambling is permitted, which would effectively bar online casino gaming. The text is silent on whether sports betting must be in-person or may be mobile.

Subpara. (e)(4) tax: the rate is fixed at 20 percent of gross income, less operating expenses allowed by law, winnings paid, and reserves permitted by law. The proceeds go to the Georgia Gaming Proceeds Fund. Other regulatory proceeds, such as fees, first fund the commission's operating expenses and reserves, and any remainder goes to the Fund.

Subpara. (e)(5) allocation: the first $2 billion is split evenly among all counties. After that, the first $500 million of each fiscal year's additional proceeds goes evenly to counties until at least $5 billion more has been paid out. At least 5 percent of the remaining proceeds must fund problem-gambling prevention and treatment. The Fund sits outside the general fund and lottery allocation rules, and under (e)(6) appropriations do not lapse.
Section 2: the measure goes to voters under Art. X, Sec. I, Para. II, with the question whether the General Assembly may provide by law for sports betting and casino gambling.
GA-SR131.comparison: Unlike the statutory mobile-wagering frameworks in AK HB145/SB194 and HI HB1308, HB2570 and SB1569, SR131 creates no operative licensing regime itself; it is a constitutional enabling amendment that still needs voter ratification and later implementing legislation. It is also unusual in locking a tax rate (20 percent) and a revenue distribution formula into the constitution. Illinois bills such as HB2878 (a $15 million master license fee) and HB3159 (a 2 percent add-on for fire and EMS) adjust an existing statute and can be changed by ordinary legislation. Its express ban on off-site casino gambling also runs opposite to iGaming authorizations such as IL HB3080 and HB4797.
GA-SR131.watch: Watch three things: the constitutionally fixed 20 percent rate and its unusual net base, since the operating expenses 'allowed by law' will be defined in implementing legislation; the 'no off-site casino gambling' clause, which forecloses iGaming; and whether enabling legislation permits statewide mobile sports betting given the one-license-per-entity ownership limit, which is drafted for casino licenses but could be extended.

IA-HF2089.summary: HF2089 amends Iowa Code section 99F.6(4)(a)(2) to require casino licensees, when making their existing mandatory charitable distributions (at least 3% of gambling-game adjusted gross receipts and 0.75% of sports wagering net receipts), to direct at least 75% of those moneys pro rata to Iowa counties based on where contributing players reside. It imposes new player-residency recordkeeping, an annual public report to the Racing and Gaming Commission, and civil penalties and license discipline for noncompliance.
mechanics: Does not change the existing 3% AGR and 0.75% sports wagering net receipts charitable distribution floors; new subparagraph division (b) governs how at least 75% of the required distribution is allocated by county.

County share equals gross receipts from players residing in that county divided by gross receipts from players in all Iowa counties; receipts from nonresidents or players whose county cannot be verified are spread proportionally on the same formula.
Licensees must collect and maintain records of the county of residence of all players or participants and the receipts attributable to each, covering both gambling games and sports wagering.
Annual report to the commission, posted publicly, covering receipts by county, nonresident and unverified receipts, total distributions, and per-county distributions.

Enforcement: civil penalty up to 5% of the total required distribution, deposited in the general fund; the commission may order redistribution; willful or repeated failure may lead to additional discipline including license suspension.
Applies to receipts collected in fiscal years beginning on or after the Act's effective date. The 25% remainder stays distributable as otherwise allowed by law.
IA-HF2089.comparison: No comparable bills from other states were listed. What is unusual is that it ties a licensee's charitable giving to player geography, effectively mandating player-level residency tracking. That is straightforward for online sports wagering accounts with KYC data but hard for anonymous retail casino and slot play. The penalty is measured against the whole required distribution, not just the misallocated portion.
IA-HF2089.watch: Watch the player-level county-of-residence tracking requirement, which is hard to meet for anonymous retail gaming. Its interaction with existing operating-agreement distribution terms is also unclear, since the bill's 75% rule is not expressly limited by the "unless an operating agreement otherwise provides" clause. Licensees also face penalty exposure of up to 5% of total required distributions plus possible license suspension.

HI-SB3263.summary: SB3263 CD1 creates a University of Hawaii name, image, and likeness framework under HRS chapter 304A. It affirms student-athletes' right to earn NIL compensation, requires UH to adopt NIL policies, sets up third-party deal disclosure and annual legislative reporting, and establishes a NIL endowment fund seeded with tuition-fund, general-fund, and matching private money. The only gaming hook is §304A-C(c)(3), which lets UH bar student-athletes from NIL deals involving gambling or sports wagering.
mechanics: §304A-C(c) permits, but does not require, UH to prohibit NIL agreements involving adult entertainment, firearms, gambling or sports wagering, illegal drugs, tobacco or vaping, or any industry conflicting with the university's mission or financial interests.
§304A-C(d) gives student-athletes at least ten business days after signing any institutional or third-party NIL agreement to rescind it.

§304A-D(a) requires student-athletes to disclose third-party NIL agreements worth $600 or more, or an alternative NCAA or federal threshold UH designates. Disclosed records are confidential and exempt from chapter 92F. Annual aggregate reports to the legislature begin with the 2028 session.

§304A-G endowment: $4M transferred from the UH tuition and fees special fund, $2.5M general-fund appropriation for FY2026-27 (Section 5, effective July 1, 2026), and $5M in university matching gifts. The corpus has a stated $10M minimum, and interest may be spent once the corpus has held $7.5M for three years.
The Act takes effect on approval and sunsets June 30, 2030, with legislative review planned for the 2029 session. Unexpended fund balances lapse to their source.
HI-SB3263.comparison: Unlike MD HB518 (college athlete protections inside a problem-gambling bill), CT HB05229 (restricting gaming advertising on college campuses) and TN SB1662 (funding athletic programs from a fee on sports wagering vendors), Hawaii's bill is a pure NIL statute. It touches wagering only through a discretionary university power to exclude gambling sponsors. It is closer to the NIL bills in WI AB1034, TX HB126, NE LB370 and NH HB312, but unusual in pairing a post-House-settlement framework with a state-seeded NIL endowment and a hard 2030 sunset. Because Hawaii has no legal sports betting, the gambling-sponsorship carve-out has limited immediate commercial effect.
HI-SB3263.watch: Watch whether UH exercises its §304A-C(c)(3) discretion to adopt a blanket ban on gambling and sports-wagering NIL deals, since that policy could become a template for other states and would bar operator endorsements with UH athletes if Hawaii ever legalizes sports betting.

IL-HB1075.summary: Illinois's Fiscal Year 2026 Budget Implementation Act (Public Act 104-0002) makes the statutory changes needed to carry out the FY2026 budget across many state programs, including agency powers, fund transfers, fund dissolutions and grant program tweaks. In the portion of the text provided, gaming appears only as a source of transfers into the Audit Expense Fund. The text supplied is truncated partway through State Finance Act Section 6z-27, so later articles cannot be assessed here.
mechanics: Section 5-30 amends 30 ILCS 105/6z-27 to order transfers into the Audit Expense Fund within 30 days after July 1, 2025. The schedule shown includes Sports Wagering Fund $14,696, State Gaming Fund $216,475, Horse Racing Fund $233,685, Illinois Gaming Law Enforcement Fund $1,411 and State Lottery Fund $106,169. The text as provided mixes stricken and new schedules, so treat these figures as indicative.

Section 5-5 gives the Department of Central Management Services authority to procure 'site readiness work' (abatement, remediation, demolition, title and environmental reports) for surplus state real property, under new 20 ILCS 405/405-217.

Section 5-10 raises the SBIR/STTR Phase I matching grant cap from $50,000 to $75,000. It also adds Phase II matching grants of up to $250,000, subject to appropriation, with a lifetime limit of 2 awards.

Section 5-25 reallocates the $4-per-car-year insurer assessment from July 1, 2025: 10% to the State Police Law Enforcement Administration Fund, 10% to the State Police Vehicle Fund and 80% to the Law Enforcement Training Fund.

Section 5-10 dissolves the Small Business Environmental Assistance Fund into the Clean Air Act Permit Fund on July 1, 2025, and Section 5-30 repeals its State Finance Act listing effective January 1, 2026.
IL-HB1075.comparison: No other states' bills are listed for comparison. On its own, this is a general budget implementation omnibus. In the text provided, wagering-related funds appear only as line items in the routine Audit Expense Fund sweep, not as changes to sports wagering tax rates, licensing or operations. Those changes, if any, would sit in separate FY2026 revenue legislation not shown here.
IL-HB1075.watch: Because the supplied text cuts off mid-Section 6z-27, review the remaining articles of P.A. 104-0002 for any further transfers from, or diversions of, the Sports Wagering Fund or State Gaming Fund, or other amendments touching the Sports Wagering Act or Illinois Gambling Act.

IL-HB111.summary: This is Governor Pritzker's June 16, 2026 veto message returning Illinois HB 111, the FY 2027 appropriations act, with item and reduction vetoes totaling $500,418,129,782, and approving all other appropriations. The vetoes correct lines the House and Senate sponsors (Rep. Gabel and Sen. Sims) identified as erroneous or duplicative. Nearly the entire total comes from one typographical line, Article 52, Section 285, enacted at $500,250,000,000. The message contains no sports-betting or gaming provisions on its face.
mechanics: Authority: Article IV, Section 9(d) of the Illinois Constitution of 1970 (item and reduction veto).
Total vetoed: $500,418,129,782. Of that, $500,250,000,000 is a single typographical error at Art. 52, Sec. 285, p. 430, lines 4-7.
Item vetoes hit lines in Articles 37, 41, 52, 93 and 118. Examples are Art. 93, Secs. 190, 195 and 200 ($20M, $4.5M and $30M) and Art. 52, Secs. 490 and 495 ($17.5M and $17.81M).
Reductions include Art. 15, Secs. 476 and 1295 (each cut from $17M to $1.7M), Art. 52, Sec. 140 (cut from $60M to $45M) and Art. 93, Sec. 40 (cut from $35M to $30M).

The message identifies lines only by article, section, page and line, without naming agencies, funds or purposes, so it cannot be determined from this text whether any vetoed line touches the Gaming Board or wagering-funded programs.
All other appropriations in HB 111 were approved, and the enacted act is PA 104-0464.
IL-HB111.comparison: No other states' bills are listed for comparison. What is unusual is the headline veto figure of roughly $500.4 billion, which is almost entirely one typographical line rather than a real policy cut. The vetoes were coordinated with the bill's own sponsors as technical clean-up, not adversarial line-item cuts.
IL-HB111.watch: Check the underlying enacted text of PA 104-0464 to see whether any vetoed or reduced lines, especially in Articles 52 and 93, correspond to Illinois Gaming Board operations or sports-wagering-funded appropriations, such as the Capital Projects Fund or problem gambling programs, since this veto message itself does not identify them.

IL-HB1704.summary: HB1704 amends Section 6z-27 of the Illinois State Finance Act to update the annual audit-cost sweep, directing the Comptroller and Treasurer to transfer specified amounts from roughly 250 state funds into the Audit Expense Fund within 30 days after July 1, 2025 (changed from 2024). It is a routine shell-style finance bill; gaming-related funds, including the Sports Wagering Fund, appear only as line items among the transferring funds.
mechanics: Changes the transfer trigger date from July 1, 2024 to July 1, 2025; transfers occur within 30 days or as soon as practical.

Gaming-related line items include Sports Wagering Fund $14,696; State Gaming Fund $1,997 and $216,475; State Lottery Fund $311,489 and $106,169; Horse Racing Fund $233,685; Illinois Gaming Law Enforcement Fund $1,411.
General Revenue Fund is listed twice at $17,653,153 each, and Education Assistance Fund is listed at $2,193,017 and $2,347,928; several funds appear twice in the list.
Federal and State trust funds are excluded unless trustees direct transfers; any shortfall in a listed fund is backfilled from the General Revenue Fund.
Auditor General must return any excess over actual audit costs to the originating fund on or around September 30; the Act is effective immediately upon becoming law.
IL-HB1704.comparison: No comparable bills from other states are listed. The bill is unusual only because it is a recurring Illinois audit-cost transfer vehicle. It touches sports betting only through a $14,696 draw on the Sports Wagering Fund and other modest gaming-fund draws, and it contains no substantive gaming policy. Its last action was a Rule 19(a) re-referral to the Rules Committee on 2025-04-11, which suggests it is likely dormant or held as a shell for later amendment.
IL-HB1704.watch: Because this is a re-referred finance shell bill, watch for a floor or committee amendment that repurposes it to carry larger sweeps from the Sports Wagering Fund or State Gaming Fund, or changes to wagering taxes, late in session.

IL-HB1451.summary: HB1451 amends the Illinois Substance Use Disorder Act to fold gambling disorder more fully into the Department of Human Services' prevention, treatment, licensing and grant authority, largely by adding 'or gambling disorders' throughout the Act. It expands the Sec. 5-20 gambling disorder program to include a toll-free hotline and website, stigma-reduction awareness and suicide-prevention efforts. It also requires each master sports wagering licensee to display a DHS-determined help statement on its portal, website, or computer or mobile app.
mechanics: Sec. 1-10 adds definitions. 'Gambling disorder' means persistent and recurring maladaptive gambling behavior that disrupts personal, family, or vocational pursuits. 'Gambling' means risking money or other items of value in games of chance, expressly including video gaming and sports betting. 'Gaming' is defined separately as playing video games.

Sec. 5-20(a)-(b): subject to appropriation, DHS (or a contractor) must run a toll-free hotline and website in place of the '800' number, promote awareness of gambling disorder impacts and stigma, and use screening, crisis intervention, treatment and training to reduce gambling-related suicide attempts.

Sec. 5-20(c): DHS determines a statement on obtaining help with a gambling disorder. Licensed gambling establishment owners must post it, and master sports wagering licensees must include it on their portal, website, or app. The provision cross-references Sec. 25.95 of the Sports Wagering Act, among other gaming statutes, for DHS-supplied signage.

Sec. 5-20(d)-(e): DHS may produce prevention literature and curricula, advise State and local officials, and support prevention projects. It may also award grants for local prevention, recognition, response and treatment programs to local health departments, correctional institutions, hospitals, universities, community-based organizations and faith-based organizations, funded by appropriations or outside grants.
Sec. 15-5: makes it unlawful to provide treatment for gambling disorders without a DHS license, extending existing substance use treatment licensure to gambling treatment providers.

Sec. 10-10 and 10-15: the Advisory Council gains duties on gambling disorder prevention, including preventing 'gambling behaviors while gaming by minors', and its public members include representatives of gambling disorder treatment programs. No new tax, fee or operator funding obligation and no effective date appear in the provided text, which is truncated.
IL-HB1451.comparison: Unlike the Hawaii sports wagering bills (HI HB 1308, HB 2570, SB1569), which create problem gambling programs as part of a full legalization, licensing and tax package, IL HB1451 is a standalone public-health bill inside an existing legal market. It imposes no tax or fee earmark. It also lacks the direct operator conduct rules in CT HB05229 (withdrawal timing, customer service lines, AI-targeting ban) and Indiana HB1078's voluntary exclusion and HB1092's child-support withholding mechanisms. Its only direct operator obligation is displaying a DHS-determined help statement.
IL-HB1451.watch: Watch the content, placement and formatting DHS sets for the required help statement on master sports wagering licensees' websites and apps under Sec. 5-20(c), and whether later amendments add an operator-funded assessment to pay for the expanded, appropriation-dependent programs.
